THE LATE HON. J. A. GLEN DEATH OF FORMER SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE   EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AND SYMPATHY
speechtext:
I am sure all hon. members have learned with deep regret of the passing of the Hon. J. A. Glen, Speaker of the House of Commons from 1940 to 1945.
Mr. Glen was elected to the house first in 1926 as member of parliament for Marquette. He was defeated in the general election of 1930, but was re-elected in 1935, 1940 and 1945. In 1940 Mr. Glen was elected Speaker of the house, and in April, 1945, joined the cabinet of Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King as Minister of Mines and Resources. He was a good administrator and a faithful and loyal member of the government to which he belonged.
In 1948 Mr. Glen was appointed to the international joint commission, and he was chairman of the Canadian section at the time of his death.
Those of us who were here when Mr. Glen was Speaker recall the fair and impartial manner in which he presided over our deliberations. During the difficult days of the war he occupied, with dignity and in the best traditions of those who had gone before him, the position which I now hold.
Mr. Glen had not been well recently, but he endured his illness with a courage and fortitude which deeply impressed all who knew him. I know all hon. members will join with me in extending sincere sympathy to Mrs. Glen and her son.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a fellow Manitoban I want to say how much we appreciate what you have said with respect to the late Mr. Glen. I know it will be appreciated also by his friends in our province, as well as those from Manitoba who were associated with him in the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to report to the house on certain developments that have taken place in the last forty-eight hours with respect to the situation in Korea, and to outline the attitude of the Canadian government.
The house will recall that at its meeting on Sunday the security council of the United Nations termed the armed attack upon the republic of Korea as a breach of the peace, and called upon the communist forces to withdraw to the 38th parallel. It soon became apparent that this appeal would be without effect on the communist government of North Korea. Their forces continued to advance on Seoul, the capital of Korea. The United Nations commission on Korea reported that they were convinced that North Korea would pay no heed to the resolution of the security council.
When the charter of the United Nations was drawn up, it was intended that such an act of aggression would be met by the dispatch of forces put at the disposal of the security council by member governments as the result of prior agreements. However, the security council has never been able to negotiate such agreements, for reasons which I need not go into now. In these circumstances, with one link missing in the chain which has been designed to hold aggression in check, it was impossible for the security council itself to take effective action to provide military assistance to the republic of Korea. If help were to be given, the responsibility would have to be shouldered by individual members of the security council acting within the terms of the charter, but on their own initiative. In
External Affairs-Korea
this case the United States recognized a special responsibility which it discharged with admirable dispatch and decisiveness.
As hon. members will know, President Truman yesterday announced that the United States would send air and sea forces to give the Korean government's troops cover and support. I feel sure that all members of the house will applaud and support this act of high courage and firm statesmanship on the part of the government of the United States.
I think it would be appropriate, Mr. Speaker, if I read into the records of the house the statement of the president. It was as follows:
In Korea the government forces, which were armed to prevent border raids and to preserve internal security, were attacked by invading forces from North Korea. The security council of the United Nations called' upon the invading troops to cease hostilities and to withdraw to the 38th parallel. This they have not done, but on the contrary have pressed the attack. The security council called upon all members of the United Nations to render every assistance to the United Nations in the execution of this resolution. In these circumstances I-
That is, President Truman.
-have ordered United States air and sea forces to give the Korean government troops cover and support.
The attack upon Korea makes it plain beyond all doubt that communism has passed beyond the use of subversion to conquer independent nations and will now use armed invasion and war. It has defied the orders of the security council of the United Nations issued to preserve international peace and security. In these circumstances the occupation of Formosa by communist forces would be a direct threat to the security of the Pacific area and to United States forces performing their lawful and necessary functions in that area.
Accordingly I have ordered the seventh fleet to prevent any attack on Formosa. As a corollary of this action I am calling upon the Chinese government on Formosa to cease all air and sea operations against the mainland. The seventh fleet will see that this is done. The determination of the future status of Formosa must await the restoration of security in the Pacific, a peace settlement with Japan, or consideration by the United Nations.
I have also directed that United States forces in the Philippines be strengthened and that military assistance to the Philippine government be accelerated.
I have similarly directed acceleration in the furnishing of military assistance to the forces of France and the associated states in Indo-China and the dispatch of a military mission to provide close working relations with those forces.
I know that all members of the United Nations will consider carefully the consequences of this latest aggression in Korea in defiance of the charter of the United Nations. A return to the rule of force in international affairs would have far-reaching effects. The United States will continue to uphold the rule of law.
I have instructed Ambassador Austin, as the representative of the United States to the security council, to report these steps to the council.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the end of President Truman's statement, issued yesterday. I

External Affairs-Korea should like to point out, if I may, that although the United States government has taken this step on its own authority, it is acting not only in accordance with the spirit and letter of the charter of the United Nations, but also in pursuance of the resolution which was adopted by the security council on Sunday. This resolution, it will be remembered, called on all members of the United Nations to render every assistance in regard to its execution. It should also be borne in mind that the United States has accepted responsibility generally for the maintenance of international peace and security in the Pacific area, and specifically for the maintenance of the security of Japan as the power responsible under international agreements for the occupation of that country. Those specific responsibilities, as well as the responsibilities which are shared by all of the members of the security council-and indeed by all members of the United Nations -for maintenance of international peace and security have no doubt contributed to the decision by the United States to come at once to the aid of Korea. If any further international authorization were needed for the prompt and vigorous action which has been taken by the United States, it has been provided by the further resolution of the security council which was passed last night recommending that the members of the United Nations furnish such assistance to the republic of Korea as may be necessary to repel the armed attack and to restore international peace and security in the area concerned. That resolution was passed by a vote of seven in favour, one against, and two delegations non-participating because they had not at that time received instructions in regard to this matter.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Which country voted against it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The government of Yugoslavia, which had produced a resolution of its own in this matter, voted against the United States resolution. The representatives of India and Egypt had not at that time last night received instructions. I understand they expect those instructions during the course of the day. The U.S.S.R., of course, took no part in the meeting, and the other delegations voted in favour of the resolution.
Possibly I should put on Hansard this extremely important resolution of the security council. It reads as follows:
The security council,
Having determined that the armed attack upon the republic of Korea by forces from North Korea constitutes a breach of the peace;
Having called for an immediate cessation of hostilities; and

Having called upon the authorities of North Korea to withdraw forthwith their armed forces to the 38th parallel; and
Having noted from the report of the United Nations commission for Korea that the authorities in North Korea have neither ceased hostilities nor withdrawn their armed forces to the 38th parallel and that urgent military measures are required to restore international peace and security; and
Having noted the appeal from the republic of Korea to the United Nations for immediate and effective steps to secure peace and security;
Recommends that the members of the United Nations furnish such assistance to the republic of Korea as may be necessary to repel the armed attack and to restore international peace and security in the area.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the resolution of the security council on this matter. As hon. members know, Canada is not now a member of the security council and therefore no decision on our part was required yesterday in regard to this resolution; but I am sure that the house will support, as indeed does the government, the action taken by the security council, because it represents collective action through the United Nations for peace.
It is the firm hope of the Canadian government, as I am sure it is the firm hope of all members of this house and of the Canadian people, that this action which has now been taken by the security council and by the United States government in conformity with the resolutions of the security council will soon end the war in Korea and thereby make possible a fresh attempt to compose the differences which have long kept that country in a state of tension and unrest, and which have led to the present outbreak of hostilities.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the house listened with keen interest and with unqualified approval to the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) indicating the government's policy with respect to support of the security council's decision and the action taken by the United States of America. Perhaps the minister might indicate to the house what that support he has mentioned as having been given by this government may mean when translated into practical terms.
I rose only to indicate that in a matter so serious and so vital to the peace and security of the world as the unprovoked aggression of the North Korean communist forces upon the South Korean territory, the people of Canada, having in mind their great desire for freedom, as they have so often expressed it and fought for it, would expect this kind of support to be given by the Canadian government. I was glad to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs express it in the terms that he used.
I want to say to the government through you, Mr. Speaker, that when it comes to a

question of such international importance and concern as this, in the twilight between peace and war-to use the expression that the minister used on a previous occasion-all of us in this parliament have a sense of unity of purpose which I hope does credit to the representatives of the Canadian people at large.
On the question of foreign affairs this parliament has sought to speak with a united voice. On an occasion so important and serious as this I want to say that when the preservation of peace itself is at stake, the government can count upon the wholehearted and unanimous support of the opposition in any measures that can be taken which are proper in the circumstances for the preservation of that peace and security. After all, when the vital issues of peace and war are before us there are no divisions in the parliament of Canada. We speak as Canadians rather than as groups divided superficially on party lines. I want to say to the government that we are prepared to lend such support as an opposition can lend in a situation such as this. We hope that the action taken, as the minister pointed out a few moments ago, so rapidly and so decisively by the United States government under the aegis of the United Nations will in the end, indeed in a very short time, bring peace to that area and solve one of the problems which face a troubled world.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I know this matter should not be discussed at this time, but I should like to express my appreciation of what the hon. member for Peel has said, and for the spirit behind his words. He directed a question to the government as to what action we are taking to implement the words of my statement. I should like to point out to him and to the house that we have not yet even received the security council's resolution formally; we saw the text of it last night. I can assure him and the house that we shall be conferring, through the United Nations, with other members of the United Nations as to what part we in Canada can and should take in any future action that may be necessary.

speechtext: May I ask the minister to tell us what action has been taken by the other governments? For example, we read in the press that the United Kingdom has already taken action. Can the minister tell us what the situation is?

speechtext:
1.	What products can be manufactured from sawdust of mills?
2.	What industries are manufacturing such products in Canada?
3.	What are the market conditions for the said products?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PRODUCTS MANUFACTURED FROM SAWDUST
speechtext:
1.	Wallboard; composition flooring; sugars; ethyl alcohol; yeast; molasses; charcoal, acetic acid and methanol; fuel briquettes (sawdust is also used, without any treatment, as a fuel); floor sweeping compound; wood flour -plastics, explosives, linoleum, wallpaper; soil conditioner; animal bedding; packaging material; insulating material; traction product for ice and snow..
There are a number of other uses for sawdust in which only insignificant quantities are consumed. These are not listed above.
In uses for sawdust for such purposes as animal bedding, insulation material, soil conditioner, and packaging, the sawdust is procured from a large number of sources and *normally by individual users, who collect direct from saw mills.
2.	Only a very few of the products listed in the answer to question No. 1 are being produced in Canada from sawdust. The more important are:
Wall'board-produced from sawdust in the maritimes by one lumber mill.
Composition flooring-produced in Ontario by one plant.
Fuel briquettes-produced by several lumber mills in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
Floor sweeping compound-produced by a number of firms.
Wood flour-^prepared by one Ontario mill.
3.	Wallboard and composition flooring have at the present time a good market due to the high level of building activity.
Fuel briquettes are used extensively as heating and cooking fuel in the vicinity of manufacture. At areas distant from the source of supply, high transportation costs limit their use to special luxury purposes such as in open fireplaces.
Floor sweeping compound is in reasonably good demand.
Wood flour has a number of outlets. However, the specification requirements of the final products are so exacting as to make successful manufacture rather difficult and highly specialized.

speechtext:
I should like to say a word about the work of the custodian of enemy property. I do not find any separate item for that, and this would appear to be the only point at which the subject can be discussed.

For at least two years I have been interested in this matter on behalf of a number of persons who suffered actual loss of their property through the action of enemy governments during the war. In some cases they suffered personal privations and hardships through their being interned, mainly in the hands of the Japanese in the Far Eastern theatre.
A large number of these people who have claims arising from damage sustained at the hands of enemy governments are in straitened financial circumstances as a result of the calamity that overtook them. I have in mind retired persons, for instance, living in the Far East, and I would refer particularly to one typical example, that of a lady who was interned with her husband, and whose husband died as a result of the treatment he received while interned. These retired and elderly people lost everything they possessed, and are not now in a position to start over again to restore their circumstances. They are suffering genuine financial hardship and distress; yet their claims have not been dealt with by the custodian of enemy property. So far as one can make out, no real progress has been made in setting up a system under which these claims could be dealt with, and in establishing a basis upon which they can be rejected, or accepted and eventually paid.
I appreciate the fact that there are difficulties involved. As yet there is no treaty of peace either with Germany or with Japan. The lack of progress results in great hardship to these people, which in the circumstances can only be described as heartless. I am not saying that the officials themselves or the government are doing this deliberately, or that they are heartless; but I am saying that the results flowing from a lack of policy and a lack of progress in dealing with these matters is heartless and imposes an unnecessary hardship upon the people concerned.
On May 15, as appears at pages 2518 and 2519 of Hansard, I received an answer to questions asked of the Secretary of State as to the total value of enemy assets held and the total amount of claims so far received. The answer I received was as follows:
Total assets in the hands of the custodian as at March 31, 1950, $51,124,833.25.
The third and fourth parts of the question were as follows:
3.	How many claims have been received from Canadians for compensation for damage suffered in the European and Far Eastern theatres of war respectively?
4.	What was the tDtal amount of those claims?

The answers were as follows:
3.	European theatres of war, 2,110 claims; Far Eastern theatres of war, 400 claims.
4.	Approximately, $65,000,000.
The assets in the hands of the custodian total $51,124,833. They do not fall far short of covering the total amount of all the claims received. I suppose it is fair to assume that when a policy outlining the basis on which these claims will be accepted and paid is worked out and applied, there will be a reduction in the total amount of the claims, and as a result the claims to be paid will be more in line with the total value of the assets now in the hands of the custodian.
Under the circumstances it is nothing short of heartless not to set in motion now some machinery by which . these people who are suffering hardship can be paid at least a portion of their claims. In the United States a commission has been set up to adjudicate on claims by persons interned during the war, and they are to be paid at the rate of $2 per day for each day of internment. Incidentally I might say that we have no similar provision in Canada. Not only have the United States made that provision, but they are making an interim payment to those whose claims have been recognized by the government.
The United States have not yet made final provision for the basis upon which claims will be paid, and as to the property out of which they will be paid, for the reason that there is not yet a treaty with Japan or Germany. But they have recognized that failure to pay imposes a hardship, and are making an interim payment. Those payments are secured and will eventually be returned to the treasury out of enemy assets held in the United States or on behalf of the United States.
It is imperative that we institute a similar process in this country. The principles could be worked out on which claims for war damage will be recognized and paid. There are 2,510 claims, and the total amount of the payments that would eventually be made could be determined. Having established that we would know how much would have to be paid out eventually, and, depending upon whether or not the total amount of the claims was covered by the $51 million of enemy assets in the hands of the custodian, we would know whether the claims as recognized could be paid in full or not.
It should be possible to make an interim payment of at least twenty-five per cent, which would be secured by the value of enemy assets in our hands. Unless we are to continue a heartless and indifferent attitude toward the suffering of these people, some program must be instituted. It may be years
Supply-Secretary of State before a treaty of peace is signed with Germany and Japan, and no one should be condemned to suffer because such treaties have not been signed. We all know that it is the fault of the Russians; and no Canadian should suffer for that reason. We know we have the assets. I am sure all hon. members would appreciate it if the Secretary of State would indicate what progress is being made in connection with this matter.

That is wliat I thought. I want to raise a question which has been raised by a good many organizations across Canada, and which no doubt has been brought to the attention of the minister from time to time. It has to do with two of our national holidays, May 24, known as Victoria day, and July 1, known as Dominion day. These are the only two I desire to discuss at the moment.
There is a feeling in some quarters that these statutory holidays might properly be observed on the nearest Monday in each case.
I suppose this has provoked about as much general discussion across Canada as almost anything else in recent years. I know there are arguments on both sides; no doubt for sentimental reasons many people will feel that there should be no change, but I wonder if the Secretary of State and the government might not give consideration to fixing the date for the celebration of Queen Victoria's birthday as the Monday nearest May 24, and similarly in the case of Dominion day. The minister might take this suggestion into consideration; I mention it only because so many organizations and citizens across Canada seem to favour the change, and I thought someone should raise the question at this time.
The other matter I want to bring up is of considerable importance; I spoke to the minister about it last session. I have no desire to go into it in any detail at this stage of the session, beyond saying that with business in the position it is, with our commerce expanding generally, the efficient, speedy issuance of patents becomes very important. The patent office is definitely linked with some of the most important branches of business in Canada. Our scientific achievements are well known and recognized throughout the world. We have some of the best scientists, some of the best inventors and many of the best brains in the world when it comes to science and its application to industry and business generally.
Whatever may have been the reasons advanced in the past for not giving aggressive leadership to bring the patent office up to date, it seems to me that now there should be a concerted drive under the leadership of the minister and the government to bring this about. It is a long way behind. I am not going to compare it with the patent offices of the United Kingdom or the United States, except to say that some years ago a concerted drive was made in the United Kingdom and the work of the patent office was brought up to something approaching a current level.
I am not going to say there is not a backlog there, because I take it that in patent work a backlog must be expected. The United


States was a good many years behind, but I understand that not so long ago they made a concerted effort and had substantial results in reducing the arrears of patent applications.
It has not been my privilege to act as a patent attorney, but I have spoken to those who have practised that profession. They have a great deal of sympathy for the commissioner and the other officials, whom they hold in high regard, but they say the whole staff have become discouraged because they are not able to keep up with the current work, let alone whittle down the backlog that has accumulated over the years. In these remarks I want to make it clear that I am not criticizing those officials, who are working hard and conscientiously, but I do criticize the government, the minister, and those who should have been trying to put the patent office on a proper footing. I do not think there is any branch of any government department that should call forth such vigorous condemnation of government policy as the patent office. There is no excuse for having let this matter simply dawdle along, to use a street expression. I had hoped that five years after the end of the war this office would have been modernized and brought up to date, but that has not been done. I am told that some patent applications which were filed back in the thirties have not yet received proper attention because of the conglomeration and congestion of work; that the backlog is so bad today that they are in arrears a minimum of five years, and in some cases much longer.
That is not the whole story. Because they are so far behind and because there are so many applications, it takes that much longer to search through all the unclassified applications which have not been attended to, when new applications are made. Fuel is added to the fire, insult is added to injury every day the patent office is permitted to continue as it is today. I do not think the public realize what this means to Canada and to business, because the patent office is unknown to most Canadians, who of course are not all inventors. Nevertheless the situation in the patent office id directly interfering with progress in the application of scientific discoveries to business and commerce in general. I do not think a government department should be in the position of having to admit that five years after the end of the war the patent office has not been modernized and brought up to date. I suppose the minister will say it is difficult to get patent examiners or other necessary staff. Somehow or other the other departments get these people.
In what sort of position does industry find itself when its scientists, in attempting to find

new formulae or inventions, realize that their competitors in other parts of the world are able to get a patent through and be in competition long before the five years which it takes an application to be dealt with by this office? I say five years, but that is only the minimum; there are many applications that take a great deal longer than that. The government ought to be aroused to the importance of this matter. I am not anxious to thresh old straw or cry over spilt milk, but, year in and year out, those of us on this side of the house have pleaded, urged, condemned -we have done everything we could to get this patent office into better shape. An end does come to the patience of the people of Canada and of the members of the house who want to see something constructive done. It is not enough to say that the patent office is moving into new quarters; it is not enough to say that they are handling more than they did. It is important for the government to announce a new policy with respect to the patent office, and to bring it up to date.
I hope the minister will be able to tell us that a new drive has been made, and that industry in Canada in the years to come will be able to look forward to the prompt treatment of applications for patents. The government has a definite responsibility to business and to applicants for patents; that responsibility is not being discharged. I suggest to the minister that before we meet in another session he should be able to announce the implementation of a new policy with respect to the patent office which will give industry a fair break.

Mr. Chairman, first of all, with reference to the member's inquiry about Victoria day and Dominion day, I may say that that question has been under consideration by several of my predecessors and myself. There seems to be a good deal of difference of opinion about it, and I suggest to the hon. member that if he wants to try it out he should introduce a private bill.
As to the patent office, I know that this house-I do not say this by way of criticism of the hon. member's remarks, but it is a fact-has used the patent office as a football from time to time. Perhaps there was some reason for that. I do not believe hon. members generally quite understand the difficulties with which this office has to contend, and with which in fact other patent offices are faced. As a matter of actual fact ours is not the only office with a backlog. The United Kingdom has a substantial backlog, as has the United States. In the year 1948, which is the only year for which I have a comparison, we did dispose of seventy-five 55946-269
Supply-Secretary of State per cent of the applications, while our friends across the border managed to dispose only of thirty-three per cent.
There are delays in connection with the issuance of patents, I know. I believe the average period between the application for a patent and the issuance of it is somewhere in the neighbourhood of three years. Please do not lay all the responsibility for that at the door of the patent office. Frequently, very frequently indeed, those delays are caused not by the office but by the applicants themselves, who in many cases make their applications and prefer to wait until they have had an application granted in either the United States or the United Kingdom, as the case may be, and then perhaps amend their own application here to bring it in line with the patent which has been issued to them in the other country.
I know it is a simple matter to talk about speeding up the work of the patent office, but I should, like to point out to the hon. member for Peel that if we proceed to speed up the work of the patent office too quickly, we shall only succeed in slowing the work. A great deal of the work, as my hon. friend is aware, in connection with this office is the work of the examiners. They are the key men to the whole process, and their work covers considerable time. They have to be highly trained men. Most of them, if not all, are engineers. In order to speed up our work we must of necessity bring in new men and train them. The more men we bring in to train, the more we slow up the work. We have to maintain a reasonable proportion between the men that we have and those that we bring in to train. This year we have already, I think, brought in eleven men. The staff of examiners now totals about forty. We cannot bring in any more men to train just now, because if we do we shall slow up the work.

I presume he receives reports from somebody, but I should like to point out to him that there are substantial difficulties in dealing with the employees of the-printing bureau, not because they are a more belligerent type of employee than any other, but because we have there two, yes three, types of employees. In the first place there are the civil servants; then we have the prevailing rates men, and even they are subdivided into various groups, from highly skilled labour to the ordinary labourer. It is not always easy to adjust the notions of unionist hourly paid labour to monthly civil servants, and the king's printer has considerable difficulty in that respect.
We try as best we can to adjust things to meet the convenience of our various employees but it must be borne in mind that the department has at least some rights, and we must adjust holidays in such a way as not to interfere with the production of the bureau.
It is quite true that there was a notice issued, as my hon. friend points out, in connection with holidays, which in itself, if it had been agreed to, would I think have been excellent from the point of view of production in the department. Of course the bureau has been operating for a number of years. Conditions of work and holidays, and so forth, have been changing from time to time. Possibly, having regard to the practice of the past, this may have been a little bit too drastic a change to make at the time; but it must also be borne in mind that the employees themselves, while they have some rights, I presume, as to when they should take their holidays, and at least should be given consideration cannot be permitted to take their holidays whenever they please. Some regard must be had to efficiency, and the production-of the department; because it is so easy in a department of that kind, where the work of one man is dependent on the work of a man in the line immediately ahead of him, to-throw the whole system out of gear and reduce production tremendously. I think, however, we have been working the matter out fairly well during the past three or four weeks, and I am optimistic enough to think that the difficulty which my hon. friend has. heard of will be overcome.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe when this matter was considered before I moved the adjournment of the debate. I should like now to try to sum up the case which I suggested that evening had not yet been dealt with.
Let me make it clear at the outset that the Social Credit party in the house realizes, as do all others, that the railways might need increased revenue to meet increased costs. We are' not arguing that at all. If that is so, then the railways ought to have the increased revenue. But we say that no increase in freight rates should be allowed until such time as a mutually satisfactory railway freight rates policy is devised and laid down. That has not yet been done.

The board of transport commissioners is not the body to lay down policy. Evidently the government has been attempting to use it either for that purpose, or merely as a body to whom they might pass the buck when they get into difficulty-a sort of shock body.
The function of laying down policy is that of the government and parliament, and not that of the board of transport commissioners. I do not intend to belabour the board or to say unkind things about it. It might well be that the biggest reason why the iniquitous discrimination in the Canadian freight rate structure has been allowed to continue is that the board have never been given any clear and adequate directive by the government, by this department, by statute, or in any other way. Certainly they have not exercised any initiative of their own.
The act under which the freight rates structure is set out and under which it operates does not contain any clear statement of policy to guide the board. For that reason the board find it convenient to follow the practices of the past, as they have grown up, in a rather haphazard manner. I do not think any body can claim honestly that our freight rate structure was built up in a comprehensive way, and based upon the principle of justice and non-discrimination and in the full light of facts that obtained at the time the freight rates were established.
I think as a matter of fact that almost anyone who has made a study of the situation must admit at once that the Canadian freight rate structure has developed on a piece-meal basis, and that actually there have grown up in Canada five main rates territories which correspond to the five main geographical regions of the country. For example we have the Ontario region, which has its rates; the maritime territory, which has its rates; the Ontario-Superior region, the prairie region, and the Pacific region. Those are the five, and each has its freight rate structure.
The eastern rates are rankly discriminatory against the western regions. In his speech the other day the hon. member for Lethbridge pointed out some examples, and I shall add to them so as to bring the information up to date. We advocate the removal of regional discrimination as a first step in the effort to give justice to consumers in all parts of Canada, as well as to put the railways in such a position that their revenues will adequately cover their requirements.
It must not be forgotten that shippers, with the exception of farmers, are in a position to pass on their freight rate costs to the ultimate consumers. Everyone knows therefore that
Supply-Transport
the consumer has to bear the full weight of any increase granted in freight rates. I might point out here incidentally that the farmer is the only one who pays his freight rates both going and coming. That is something that must be considered when this whole question of freight rates is studied. I am concerned about the position of the board in this matter. I am convinced that the board simply cannot remove these regional discriminations and introduce the principle of equalization without clear and precise direction laid down by the government in the railway statute, because to do so would be for the board to presume that it has the right to lay down policy. The minister and his colleagues must know that the board has not the right to lay down policy. I think that it was a recognition of that principle that led the original framers of the Railway Act to put in section 52, which placed upon the government not only the right but the responsibility to take action when direction is needed by the board.
There is no statutory direction to the effect that there must be no regional rate discrimination, and for that reason the board has doubtless felt that its main job in the matter of freight rates is to prevent unjust personal discrimination or undue preference within a region. That seems to be the principle which has guided them thus far and the tradition upon which they work whenever a reference is made to them. I must say that consistently and constantly the board have been actuated by tradition and not by good sense or judgment.
In 1925 the government of Canada appeared to have realized that what I have just stated was true, and in that year they passed order in council P.C. 886, which made explicit reference to the equalization of freight rates as a matter of government policy. I should like to quote from the directive given by the committee of the privy council to the board, as follows:
The committee therefore advise that the board be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rate structure of railways and railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit of the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of the dominion and the expansion of its trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of its agricultural and other basic industries. . . .
However, in the general freight rates investigation that ensued, the directive from the government to the board in connection with equalization was followed only to the extent of prescribing that branch line rates on grain in western Canada should be equal

Supply-Transport
to main line rates. The difference between standard class rates and tariff rates in western Canada was left unchanged, and the mountain differential was not removed. In my judgment the pity was that the government of the day made no changes whatever in the act which would give specific directions to the board.
I should like to refer to another order in council, P.C. 1487, passed on April 7, 1948, containing another directive to the board of transport commissioners on the same subject of the equalization of freight rates. I should like to quote briefly the directive part of that order in council, to show how similar it was to the one passed in 1925, and to show that no more could be done under that directive than could be done in 1925. It reads:
The committee also observe that since decision was rendered upon the Investigation referred to in the preceding paragraphs, namely by judgments of the said board of September, 1927, many changes have taken place in the economy of Canada and it is therefore advisable that the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rates structure of railways and railway companies which are under the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rates structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities so as to permit the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of Canada and the extension of Canadian trade both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of agriculture and other basic industries.
The committee, accordingly, advise that the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada be directed to undertake a general freight rates investigation along the lines indicated in the preceding paragraph subject to such special statutory provisions as affect freight rates-
Those last words render the directive absolutely useless. The same thing will happen as happened after a similar directive was passed in 1925. The board will find it impossible to remove regional or other discriminations. The failure of the board in 1925 and thereafter to make specific progress toward equalization as a result of the general review of freight rates that took place then emphasized the need for a change in the Railway Act if any particular change in policy is to be accomplished by which effective equalization steps can be taken.
With regard to statutory regulations, we in this corner of the house have advocated constantly two guiding principles that ought to be in the minds of the government and the board. The first is that the general form of the rate structure should be prescribed by statute and not be allowed to rest in the hands of a board that is guided almost solely by tradition. The responsibility of the board then would be, and ought to be, to maintain
TMr. Low.]
the form, laid down by the sovereign power in this country, the representatives of the people in this parliament.
The second guiding principle is that the regulations and rates should be governed in the main by standards of comparison which do not go beyond the rates themselves. When that sort of freight rate structure is built, then I maintain that the board will really have something to guide them. Until then they will not.
I would direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that the Maritime Freight Rates Act contains certain sections which illustrate the kind of change which may be required in order to establish the principle of equalization. I should like to quote briefly from section 3, subsection 2, of that act, as follows:
The board of railway commissioners, hereinafter called the board, is authorized and directed to
(a)	approve such cancellations, and, subject to the provisions of the Railway Act, respecting tariffs of tolls for the carriage of freight, where not inconsistent with this act, to approve all tariffs of tolls so substituted;
(b)	maintain or cause to be maintained such substituted tariffs, subject to all provisions of the Railway Act respecting tariffs of tolls not inconsistent with this act, on the general rate level of approximately twenty per cent below the tolls or rates existing on the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-seven, while the cost of railway operation in Canada remains approximately the same as at the said date, but the board may allow the increase or reduction of such tolls or tariffs' from time to time to meet increases or reductions, as the case may be, in such cost of operations;
(c)	adjust or vary such substituted tolls or rates from time to time as new industrial or traffic conditions arise, but always in conformity with the intent of this act as expressed in sections seven and eight and other relative sections hereof.
As a result of the specific direction given the board in that act, it is no longer necessary for a shipper in the maritimes, in making a complaint against a difference in class or commodity rates as between the maritimes and central territories, say in Ontario or Quebec, to show personal discrimination or actual detriment in order to obtain an adjustment. All the board requires is to have someone raise the question, whether he be a shipper or not, and under th'e section I have just read the board is bound to consider the complaint and shippers in the maritimes are thus given almost automatic adjustment. That is the sort of thing that ought to be in our whole freight rates structure, and that is what we are asking the government to consider.
Before I pass on I should like to emphasize that the significant part of the section which I read lies in the fact that a directive is given to the board which finds no parallel anywhere in the Railway Act, which governs

western and central railway freight rates. According to the section I read, the Board has been directed to maintain a certain relationship between the rates of the two regions, and to vary the rates in the maritime region always in conformity with the intent of the act, which was to make it possible for the maritime freight rates schedule to be twenty per cent lower.

That is fine; I respect my hon. friend's judgment. Let me make it clear again that I am not complaining about the twenty per cent compensation. I think it is coming to the maritimes. I am trying to emphasize that the government realizes that the board of transport commissioners requires a specific directive to be able to accomplish that result. So, I contend, they must give a directive to the board of transport commissioners in order to bring about the result which must be achieved if the west is to get away from these serious discriminations.
I do not believe I need say any more at the moment to convince members of the committee that responsibility for removing the discriminatory features of the present freight rate structure lies with the government itself, not with the board of transport commissioners. Whether or not we have confidence in the board, that body simply cannot do its job without a law giving it proper directions as a matter of settled policy. Let us leave it at that. The minister may want to deny this, but right now I charge the government with having used the board as a buffer when they did not want to stand up and accept their responsibility.
Western Canada is facing a shocking situation, to say the least, as a result of the freight rate increases of the past two years. The recent twenty per cent award by the board of transport commissioners is a paralysing blow to the prairie provinces, and especially to my own province of Alberta, which stands
Supply-Transport
at the very peak of the whole structure. Saskatchewan is almost as badly off, and my words now are an appeal for fair play to all the prairie provinces, which are suffering together. People have been led to believe that the recent increases were horizontal, and it will come as a shock to many that this is not so. The railways have already decided that no portion of the last twenty per cent increase will be applied to the competitive rates that exist in the western provinces. The board's orders of March 1 and May 11 of this year make that procedure quite possible, and the railways have already come to a decision in the matter. The question, then, is whether this twenty per cent increase, from which the railways expect to gather in another $29 million-

speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the argument of my hon. friend, but I am sure he does not want to make a statement that is wholly inaccurate.

I said that the railways had
already decided that no part of the twenty per cent increase would be applied to the non-competitive or normal rates.

I accept the minister's statement for the time being, but that is the information coming to me directly from the railways themselves. There is no gainsaying this; that in the board's orders of March 1 and May 11, provision is made whereby the railways can do that. I do not believe that can be denied; and if the loophole is left in the board's orders do you suppose for one moment the railways will not take advantage of it? We will leave it at that and see what happens.
Under the orders of the board the railways have the right to gather in another $29 million of revenue, and in all probability that $29 million will be added to the noncompetitive or normal rates; we will put it that way. This simply means that the whole twenty per cent increase will be paid by the people of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, with the lion's share being paid by Alberta and Saskatchewan. All the canned goods, textiles, clothing, automobiles, farm machinery, tools, furniture and a great many other necessities that go into Alberta will be subject to a large and unwarranted freight increase, and the costs of these things to the

Supply-Transport
consumers out there will take another great jump as soon as the new rates go into effect, unless this government takes counter-action following the petition presented by the provinces last week against the twenty per cent award. The government can quite properly do this under section 52 of the Railway Act. Whether or not that has ever been done, this government has done a good many things never done before, so why in the name of common sense should they fall back on a foolish argument like that?
This increase of twenty per cent will further accentuate the difference between the cost of living in eastern and western Canada. It will be simply one more tariff barrier against trade between the central provinces and the Canadian west, which is a very serious matter. Our people out there are asking with increasing frequency of late just where are those benefits that people have been talking about as accruing from confederation. If these iniquities continue there will be a greater outcry against the terms of confederation. Our people do not want anything but a unified Canada, but certainly they want fair treatment and I bespeak it for them. Again, the twenty per cent increase will apply to everything shipped out of Alberta and Saskatchewan bound for either the west coast or the east coast, with the exception of our grain. Our coal, oil, beef, pork, pottery, hides, lumber and fish will be handicapped by one more laid-down cost disability, so that the producers in those provinces will not find it possible to compete against eastern or foreign products of the same kind. I say this is a shocking situation.
Moreover, thanks to the canals built and operated free of charge by the federal government, for which our western people helped pay; and thanks to the competition provided by the Panama canal route with respect to goods shipped by way of Vancouver and the west coast, the competitive railway rates which apply in Ontario and Quebec, and also on through shipments to the west coast, will bear no portion of the twenty per cent increase. To all intents and purposes the canals were provided for Ontario and Quebec free of charge, and their operation is also provided without charge to the central provinces. As a result Alberta and Saskatchewan get it in the neck, and that is not right.
I should like to cite briefly, Mr. Chairman, some examples to illustrate how unjustly discriminatory to the west the rates have become. Let us take this one first: When the recent twenty per cent increase becomes effective, the rate on canned goods, which form a substantial part of the wintertime diet of the western people, from eastern Canada will be as follows: From Toronto to

Calgary and Edmonton, $2.77 per hundredweight; from Toronto to Vancouver, $1.40 per hundredweight; from Vancouver to Calgary and Edmonton, $1.25. Now, the rate to Calgary and Edmonton directly from Toronto and the rates from Vancouver to Calgary and Edmonton will be increased because they are normal or non-competitive rates. But the rate from eastern Canada to Vancouver, which is a competitive rate, will not be increased at all. As a result the rate to Calgary will be 197 per cent of the rate to Vancouver, although the distance to Vancouver is 500 miles greater. If that is not rank discrimination, you show me.
To make the matter look even more ridiculous, the rate from Toronto to Vancouver and back from Vancouver to Calgary or Edmonton, will be 12 cents per hundredweight less than the published rate direct from Toronto to Calgary. Talk about stupidity and being bound by tradition! Yet the the minister says there is no discrimination.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister made no such statement.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: If the minister will look at the speech he made when this subject was under discussion three weeks ago, he will see that he did.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL

I did say that there was discrimination, but there was a distinction between the discrimination as mentioned in the Railway Act and the illustrations given. The point at issue is whether there is unjust discrimination. The hon. member has been citing cases all along, none of which are proof of unjust discrimination within the meaning of the act; that is the whole point.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: That is exactly the whole point I am discussing today. I am appealing to the minister to see to it that the act is changed so that these diabolical things cannot continue.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: That matter has been referred to the royal commission. When we have the report of the royal commission, perhaps we shall be able to act in accordance with the recommendations.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: Perhaps. I am just wondering how many times we have to have royal commissions before we can get justice.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: That is what the house wanted-a royal commission.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
We wanted the act changed. We have been asking for it for years, and instead of that we get royal commissions, and reports which nobody reads-at least, no one that can do anything about it. The people in the

west are wondering if this whole thing is deliberately engineered in order that prairie points may not become distributing centres. In any event, that is the effect of it. Whether or not it is done deliberately, a good many people ask themselves just how it is engineered.
Here is another example concerning an item that is vital to farming in western Canada-tractors.	These implements are
necessary to enable the people to produce the quantities of wheat and grain that they do. Many of them come from Rock Island, Illinois. From Rock Island, Illinois, to Montreal, Quebec, which is a distance of 997 miles, in 1947 the rate was 99 cents a hundredweight. In 1950, if the last twenty per cent award is put into effect, there will be no increase on that particular haul. But from Rock Island to Neepawa, Manitoba, a distance of 1,001 miles, the rate in 1947 was $1.40 per hundredweight. When the twenty per cent increase is applied it will be $1,561, as compared with the 99 cents for a distance only four miles less. The rate to Manitoba would then be 57 per cent more for approximately the same mileage. Who can justify that sort of discrimination? If it is not unjust, I should like the minister to explain it in a way that reasonable people can understand.
For the same haul of a tractor from Rock Island, Illinois, to Quebec city, a distance of 1,170 miles, the rate is $1.10 per hundredweight. That was the charge in 1947, and that will be the rate under the new schedule, because it is a competitive rate for which there will be no increase under the twenty per cent award. The rate to Swift Current, Saskatchewan, the same mileage, in 1947 was $1.72, which is discriminatory in itself. In 1950 it will be $1.93 per hundredweight, showing a rate discrimination of seventy-five per cent against the west for exactly the same haul in miles. For hauling one of those tractors from Rock Island, Illinois, to Saint John, New Brunswick, a distance of 1,472 miles, in 1947 the rate would have been $1.25 per hundredweight. No increase will be made under the twenty'per cent award, so it will remain at $1.25. However, to Brooks, Alberta, a distance of 1,480 miles, eight miles further, in 1947 the rate was $1.96 per hundredweight. The new rate under the twenty per cent award will be $2.27J per hundredweight, showing a ninety per cent rate discrimination against the Alberta point for a haul of only eight miles further. Yet there is no unjust discrimination, the minister says. .
Let us take a shipment of binders as another illustration of this iniquitous discrimination. A binder that weighs 2,052
Supply-Transport
pounds, shipped from Hamilton, Ontario, to Saint John, New Brunswick, a distance of 1,115 miles, in 1947 took a rate of $11.39. The 1950 rate will be $16.62-that is when the twenty per cent increase is applied. For the same binder shipped to Lethbridge, Alberta, from Hamilton, a distance of 1,897 miles in 1947 took a rate of $32.82, but the 1950 rate will be $48.69. The distance from Hamilton to Lethbridge is 780 miles further than from Hamilton to Saint John, but the rate to the Alberta point is almost three times that to the New Brunswick point which indicates at least a fifty per cent discrimination against Alberta.
This is not the end. It seems, Mr. Chairman, that the railways are to be faced shortly with a further wage demand that may run into $19 million or $20 million. This will probably mean another application by the railways for freight rate increases. If the application is granted, then the non-competitive rates are likely to take another jump. The freight rate structure is breaking down before our very eyes, while the government stands idly by, passing the buck to the board of transport commissioners which is prostrated into incompetence through lack of specific direction from the government.
We in the Social Credit group hold the definite view that whenever the railways really need added revenues, and when they are unable or unwilling to apply an authorized rate increase equally to all parts of the rate structure and to all sections of Canada, then we say the time has arrived for the consolidated revenue fund to provide the amount of the increase. This would prevent the widening or aggravation of regional discrimination, that otherwise is sure to result. Surely, to call upon Alberta or any other province to pay not only its share of the rate increase, the total of which is now forty-five per cent above 1947, but also the share which the competitive rate areas escape paying, is indefensible and unjust action which can and must be corrected by providing relief to the railroads out of the public treasury. By doing this the burden of rail costs can be equitably distributed over the whole of Canada.
Unless some such action is taken, and soon, confederation may be strained very close to the breaking point, and that would be a disaster that should never be allowed to occur. I am speaking advisedly when I say that. A good many people, and I am one of them, believe that the Canadian railways are pricing themselves out of business. I am one of those who think that the railways have become complacent and lazy; that they have not kept up with the times in equipment, service or operating costs; and that is why

Supply-Transport
they are facing such strong competition from the buses and trucks in many parts of Canada. It seems to me that they ought to be following some of the policies that are being followed by certain railways in the United States. The United States rail story is told by Herbert Askwith, a New York public relations counsel who has travelled far and observed much. As a commuting New Yorker he has felt the impact of increased rail rates, so he decided to study the problem and see what he could find. And what he found is a rather scathing denunciation of what the American railways have been doing. In "Railroads on the Wrong Track", he fears that, because of ever higher rates, the railways may be heading into government ownership and socialism through loss of patronage to other forms of travel-the plane for passenger and the truck for freight. He knows the Americans wouldn't like that.
But he thinks he has found the antidote in the action of some of the western U.S. roads, the Southern Pacific and the Santa Fe in particular. As against the poor showings of the eastern roads, these western systems both made good money in 1948 by running good passenger trains and charging less per mile, and by improving their freight handling program so as to do a more efficient job for their customers. Mr. Askwith points out that while the eastern roads are charging around 3 375 cents a passenger mile one way, the Santa Fe is charging 2-41 cents a mile for a one-way ticket and just over two cents for a round trip. Southern Pacific on some of their de luxe coach passenger trains in the south and west are as low as 1-59 cents single and 1-43 cents per mile on a round trip. In April of last year the S.P.'s famous "Daylights" serving the west coast carried 10 million passengers. Fares are low because they're not running with empty seats and because they're beating plane fares. This is in contrast with what Mr. Askwith says appears to be an "unstoppable determination on the part of the eastern roads to price themselves out of the market."
That is what is happening in the United States, and that is what is happening in Canada. Then the railroads come crying to the board asking them. to stop this iniquitous bus competition and bus competition. I think it would be a tragedy if the board of transport commissioners or this government interfered until such time as the railroads have brought themselves up to date and have shown some pioneering spirit in these days.

I just want to close by making a short reference to the Crowsnest freight rate agreement. It is an agreement to hold in perpetuity. It is an agreement that must not be broken. It is an agreement which I know certain forces have been trying to have abrogated. But I will tell you that it is vital to the success of the farming operations in the west. It is vital to all our people. I will say this, Mr. Chairman. The railroads have never yet been able to show that they are not making money hauling grain under the freight rates of the Crowsnest agreement; and until such time as they do show that they are losing money, not even slight consideration should be given to any change in the policy. I listened carefully to the
speech delivered by the leader of the Social Credit party, and I wish to compliment him on his excellent presentation. I also wish to assure him that I support what he has said. As he so well pointed out, the chief fact before us today is that, with increasing railway freight rates, there is an increasing amount of discrimination. The minister himself, in a remark he has just made, underlines that fact when he says there has been a forty-five per cent increase in general rates and a forty per cent increase in competitive rates. When one considers along with that the fact that the competitive rates were initially lower, and that the percentage increase in competitive rates has been less than in other rates, then one realizes that the regular rates which are paid by us in the west and the competitive rates paid by the people in central Canada are getting farther and farther apart.
I believe it is the duty of the government to adopt a freight and rail policy which will be fair to all parts of Canada. In a country so wide and extensive it is essential that we have an adequate and efficient transportation service. We in the west have been hoping for many years to have our area industrialized to a greater extent, but with each increase in freight rates the possibility of our getting industries into that part of Canada is getting less and less.
The first increase in freight rates came about in the spring of 1948. Since that time, during almost all of that time, there has been an application before the board of transport commissioners. We know that when an application is before the board of transport commissioners we in parliament are denied the right to discuss railway freight rates.

Although this is the third increase that has taken place since last fall, we were not able until June 2 to have a general discussion on the government's freight policy and the policy adopted by the board of transport commissioners. I object to an opportunity not being given to parliament, at regular intervals, to discuss our transportation problems. It is important that we do not allow the fact that the matter is before the board of transport commissioners at any time to prevent parliament from discussing railway freight rates and transportation policies. Surely we on all sides of the house have a real responsibility in that regard.
On June 2 it was said by most speakers in that debate that the board of transport commissioners has been inadequately staffed, and that it has shown, by its various judgments and the mistakes which it has admitted, that it is incompetent. I believe that one of the commissioners, Mr. MacPherson, in the judgment of March 1, 1950, or in his statement following the judgment of the chief commissioner, frankly admitted that the board was not in a position to deal adequately with the question of discrimination. Let me quote what he said:
I concur in the judgment of the assistant chief commissioner although I would prefer to see some relief given by way of maximum increases on basic materials where the markets are long distances from the source of supply. I realize, however, that the board cannot deal with the over-all revenue requirements and limit the increase in certain cases. To do so would entail a much more complete study of individual types of traffic than the board is able to do at the present time.
In other words, Mr. MacPherson said that something should be done to remove discrimination, but the board is not in a position to undertake such a job. The government should see to it that the board of transport commissioners is adequately staffed; that it is in a position to study and to establish freight rates in Canada that are equitable to all parts. While it may be the duty of the board of transport commissioners, so far as it is possible, to remove discrimination, it certainly is the duty, obligation and responsibility of the government to remove discriminatory freight rates against any section of western Canada to which they may apply.
The government of course was quite willing to appoint a royal commission; it was quite willing to shelve its responsibility for a year. The minister has said before that the provinces were not anxious to place their case before the board of transport commissioners in relation to the general inquiry; that they wanted a royal commission. Well, that is true; but the provinces want the removal of discrimination. They
Supply-Transport
felt that from the experience they already had with the board of transport commissioners it was useless for them to go to the expense and the trouble of submitting reports for a general inquiry; they would rather take their chances on a brand new body. Of course that is why they asked for a royal commission. They asked for a royal commission in the main because they wanted the royal commission, but they asked for a royal commission also in the hope that somehow, some time, a royal commission might give some information on which the government would act to remove discrimination.
We shall soon learn whether or not the government set up the royal commission with the objective in view of removing discrimination, or whether it was set up only in order that the government might shelve its own responsibilities until the election was over, and after that to allow three further increases in freight rates, and perhaps in the future allow further increases and further discrimination to take place.
Before the royal commission has come some excellent information as to the impact of freight rates on various industries and various parts of Canada. At the sitting in Regina in June of last year, Mr. J. S. Turnbull, of the Saskatchewan dairy association, placed on record the impact of freight rates against the dairy industry in Saskatchewan. He pointed out that while the whole cost of operation in the manufacture and distribution of a pound of butter amounted to 9-92 cents, of that amount 4-97 cents was used for the payment of freight rates. In other words, the total cost in the manufacture and export of butter from the province of Saskatchewan has in it a 60 per cent cost for freight rates, which amounts to 5 cents a pound. That was before the last three increases in freight rates. We know that the price of butter has been going down because the government has set lower and lower floor prices under butter. According to the submission of Mr. Turnbull, the dairy industry in the province of Saskatchewan was in real peril back in June, 1949. Of course that peril has been increased because the price of butter itself has gone down, and there has been a further addition in cost owing to three increases in freight rates.
The Saskatchewan poultry producers informed the board that the total cost of freight going into the collection and distribution of a dozen eggs amounted to 6 cents. They pointed out that while in 1948 the eastern prices for eggs were 474 cents a dozen in the spring and 54J cents a dozen in the fall,
4270

Supply-Transport
because of freight rates and other reasons the producers in Saskatchewan received only 30 cents a dozen. Of course now the price of eggs has been reduced, the government's floor price has been reduced, and on top of the original 6 cents freight cost there have been three further freight rate increases. It is little wonder that in correspondence I get from poultry and egg producers in Saskatchewan they tell me that at the present time they are receiving only from 19 to 20 cents a dozen on the basis of average grades. That is understandable, when in 1948 they received only 30 cents a dozen.
The Canadian Co-operative Producers Limited, which is a meat processing plant located in the city of Swift Current, placed before the royal commission the effect of high and discriminatory freight rates against that industry. In his submission the secretary of that co-operative had this to say:
The net effect of increased cost was a deficit on 1948 operations of $93,663, and an examination of figures presented herein shows that discriminatory freight rates and other transportation difficulties have been mainly responsible.
In other words the high and ever-increasing cost of transportation was crippling the Canadian Co-operative Producers Limited. According to the reports submitted to the royal commission, freight costs were crippling the poultry and dairy industry in Saskatchewan. I should like to see a policy adopted that would encourage the industrialization of the prairies and the maritimes, but the government through its transportation policy, or lack of policy, allow increasing freight rate increases, increasing discrimination, and by that means not only fail to encourage industrialization in these parts of Canada, but even prevent industry already located in those areas from operating at a profit. Instead of those areas becoming further industrialized, the industry which they now have is being crippled through increased freight rates.
The government have taken this attitude: The main thing in the question of freight rates is to see that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company makes a profit. That would be the yardstick. The C.P.R. must make enough to have a reasonable margin, have a reasonable surplus and pay a reasonable dividend; we shall set freight rates in such a way that the C.P.R. will show that profit position. The government have been very successful in that regard. The C.P.R.'s profits in 1949 were $2 million higher than they were in 1948. Instead of the government making C.P.R. profits the yardstick of its transportation policy, they should make equitable freight rates their yardstick. The

government should say: We are going to have equitable freight rates, freight rates that will apply equally to all parts of Canada. Then we would find out whether the railways. make money or lose money. If they lose money, the government should consider subsidies. But the government should not say that our transportation policy is based upon profits to the C.P.R. Rather it should say that it is based upon an equitable freight rate structure, and then, if necessary, take care of the operating expenses of the railways by some other means.
The government have done something in the way of subsidies on freight rates. Feed grains going to eastern Canada from western Canada have been subsidized for a number of years. The total subsidy to date has amounted to about $139 million. It has been suggested by members from western Canada from time to time that that subsidy was one only to the eastern producers. I believe that when the government pays a subsidy on a shipment of feed grain from Fort William east, and by that means removes the freight cost, the result is beneficial not only to eastern but also to western producers.
The hon. member for Peace River has mentioned the Crowsnest pass rates, and has said that those rates should not be changed. He pointed out that if they were changed there would be the greatest possible amount of resentment shown in western Canada. I agree with him wholeheartedly in that statement. I want to point out, however, that so far as the shipment of certain grains to eastern Canada is concerned, we have something Which is just a little better than the Crowsnest pass rates. We have the Crowsnest pass rates on grain going to Fort William, and then we have free freight after that. In my opinion that is a good thing.
I am trying to say to the minister that the government is already paying a subsidy in respect of freight rates on a certain commodity. It has not entirely opposed subsidies on freight rates. I say it should now give consideration to a greater subsidy, if that is necessary-and I believe it is-in order that freight rates may be equalized from one end of Canada to the other.

In the application submitted to the board of transport commissioners the special case of the Buchans Mining Company Limited was set out. This company operates in the middle of the island and ships ore to a point to be forwarded by boat. This part of the application reads:
The annual production of concentrates of the company, amounting to approximately 130,000 long tons, is shipped by rail from Buchans via Bishops Falls to the port of Botwood on the northern coast of Newfoundland.
The company is presently paying a rate varying from $2.35 to $2.75 per ton on the movement of the concentrates from Buchans to Bishops Falls, and the schedule of rates applicable is the same as applied prior to confederation of Newfoundland with Canada.
This movement is a preferred movement under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and is entitled to a twenty per cent reduction on the basic rate under the statutory requirement of that act. The application of the act and the statutory twenty per cent reduction would result in a substantial decrease in the rate presently fixed on these concentrates. It appears that this movement has not been accorded the benefit of the act or any reduction whatsoever.
Apart from the failure to apply the Maritime Freight Rates Act in this instance, it would seem that the basic rates fixed on this concentrate movement are excessive and discriminatory. Despite the fact that, in connection with the movement of the Buchans concentrates, the Buchans Mining Company Limited furnishes all the ore cars for the movement and maintains forty-seven per cent of the trackage used in the movement and assembles all the ore trains, the freight rates chargeable by the Canadian National Railways are in excess of rates for comparable movements in other parts of Canada where all equipment is provided and track maintenance and services assumed1 by a railway.

As this is not the case, a further deduction and allowance should be made on this rate of $1.42 per ton in order to arrive at a fair basic for

the Buchans concentrates movement. When that rate Is established, the twenty per cent deduction under the Maritime Freight Rates Act would then have to be applied.

As to how the other parts of the maritimes feel about that and about the contract, I should like to refer briefly to an editorial which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of March 8, 1950, under the heading "The Terms of the Contract." It had this to say:
Newfoundland, as a result of union, is a maritime province, the fourth maritime province. And the terms of union with Newfoundland provide that "for the purpose of railway rate regulation, the island of Newfoundland will be included in the maritime region of Canada" and "through traffic moving between North Sydney and Port aux Basques will be treated as all-rail traffic." And generally, "all legislation of the parliament of Canada providing for special rates on traffic moving within, into, or out of, the maritime region will, as far as appropriate, be made applicable to the island of Newfoundland."

Certainly this discrimination is unfair and unjust.

Those are the statutes I have quoted.

We think that the obvious purpose of this subsection is-
