Of the $29,288,350 required, $25,330,550 represents salaries and the salary item compares with actual expenditures for 1949-50 of $24,891,263. There has been a major change in the composition of the salary item. When the last report to the house on estimates was made I said that the staff at

Supply-National Revenue October 31, 1949, consisted of 10,963 persons. At the end of May, 1950, this figure had declined to 10,477, composed of 5,231 permanent employees and 5,246 temporary employees. At the end of March, 1949, there were 11,704 employees, of whom 2,773 were permanent.
The estimates before you provide only for positions occupied at the time the estimates were prepared and a small number of student assistants, 210, taken on in the various district offices for the summer to assist in clearing peak-loads of work. There is a steady, continuing shrinkage in staff due largely to the introduction of new methods and procedures and to the fact that, through prodigous efforts last year, the great backlog of work accumulated during the war has been cleared. I am unable to forecast accurately what the ultimate shrinkage in personnel will amount to, but I am satisfied that it will be substantial and I hope that, by the end of the current fiscal year, I shall be in a position to make a more realistic statement as to the level at which the staff will tend to become stable.

It should be added that reductions in staff do not necessarily represent comparable reductions in dollars because there are promotions, reclassifications and salary increases occurring constantly. These are very carefully screened by the department, the civil service commission and treasury board.
The second largest item to which I should like to refer briefly represents printing, stationery and equipment for which submission is made for $1,605,000. This compares with $1,610,000 in the estimates of 1949-50 and actual expenditures of $1,258,078. Included in the estimates is an amount of $188,980 covering accounts for the 1949-50 year not rendered until after the end of the fiscal year. Expenditures under this item

consist largely of stationery and forms. As hon. members will understand, the consumption of forms is enormous. In addition to millions of personal returns, there are information returns and departmental forms of various kinds required in head office and district offices of the department in the handling of the large sums for the collection of which the department is responsible. Considerable progress has been made in eliminating unnecessary forms and in simplifying those in use. There has, however, been a constant increase in the cost of getting forms made. This work is handled through the office of the king's printer and I am satisfied that the greatest care is exercised in ensuring that the work is done at the lowest possible cost to the crown.
The third largest item in the estimates is travelling expenses. Figures for travelling are as follows:	In the estimates of 1949-50,
$1,015,500 was voted. The actual expenditures for that fiscal year were $604,708. The amount requested this year is $900,000. The amount of travelling done by officials of the department is governed almost entirely by the amount of field work done. To ensure equitable administration of the tax legislation involves a considerable amount of field work. While travelling expenses may appear to be high, I am satisfied that this amount is fully justified by the results of the work done by the officers of the department who are required to travel.
The next largest item is postage. This represents postage at the district offices. The district office postage cost covers largely communications with taxpayers, including a substantial amount of mail required to be registered. No important reduction can be anticipated in this item.
The next item to which I should like to make brief reference is legal costs. It was estimated for 1949-50 that these costs would amount to $200,000. The actual expenditures were $165,000. The amount requested this year is $200,000. The increase over the actual expenditures is due to the fact that the department expects to spend more this year in collecting overdue accounts. A program has been undertaken to ensure that taxes for 1949 and prior years will have been collected in full by the end of March, 1951. The public might as well have that known at this time. This is now possible because the assessing for those years has recently been completed and it is felt that collections must be brought into line with assessing.
I should like to add a brief word on publicity. The department's advertising costs, except for a small amount for newspaper notices, are entirely those expenditures made

by way of radio and street car advertising in the spring of each year, advising taxpayers of the requirements for filing returns and endeavouring to persuade taxpayers to get their returns in early. This publicity is of assistance to the public and at the same time accelerates the flow of returns, which means that the returns can be dealt with more efficiently in the district offices.
With the very able assistance of the comptroller of the treasury and his officers, the handling of refunds of overpayments was greatly expedited this year. Between February and June 9, some 1,599,810 cheques for $44,473,335 were issued to individual taxpayers, representing overpayments of 1949 taxes. On March 31, some 8,137 cheques for $52,436,515 were issued to corporate taxpayers, representing the refundable portion of the 1944 excess profits taxes. Those two figures give a total of $100 million which was returned promptly to Canadian taxpayers in that period.
There are still in the hands of the department some 76,665 cheques payable to individual taxpayers in respect of the refundable portion of taxes. Claims for these cheques are still coming in, but at a diminishing rate. Those cheques which have not been delivered by the end of the current fiscal year will be returned at that time to treasury for cancellation.
During the fiscal year which ended March 31, 1950, some 33,395 individual taxpayers received interest of $87,040.87. This is the first time this item has appeared in departmental accounts, following the new provisions in the Income Tax Act. The smallness of the amount in relation to the refunds made is an indication of the speed with which overpayments are now being restored to the public.

speechtext:
Once again I would like to		
express appreciation of this quite complete statement by the minister on the operations of the department, which in addition to being informative is actually a very interesting survey of the work of the taxation division. I have just one or two comments arising out of the statement. The first has to do with the amount of overpayments refunded to individual taxpayers; I believe $44 million was the figure mentioned. In that connection I think the department is entitled to a word of commendation from those of us who are sometimes critical of the work it has done in catching up with overdue assessments. I do feel that a tremendous effort has been made by the minister, and I think those of us who have urged that this be done should express our appreciation.
It seems to me the amount of the refund of overpayments would perhaps justify some of the criticism that has been [DOT] directed not to the minister but to his colleague the Minister of Finance in connection with the penalties on arrears of income tax. This $44 million refunded in overpayments would indicate that Canadians are much more prone to overpay their taxes than to deliberately underpay them. Yet I recall that in giving reasons for the quite heavy interest rate imposed as a penalty on arrears of taxes, the Minister of Finance said that was done to discourage underpayment. Certainly it cannot be said that the interest rate allowed on advance payments is any encouragement to overpay,

Supply-National Revenue so I believe it is a tribute to the honesty of the Canadian people and their desire to comply with the income tax laws to the very best of their ability; and when they err they do so on the right side. I am not going to press the point, because it concerns the Minister of Finance, but I believe it does reinforce our contention, which I still put forward, that the interest penalty on arrears of taxes is unfair and too heavy, particularly when, as in most cases, it can be clearly proved that the underpayment resulted from an error and not from any deliberate intent. I am interested in that figure; I think it will serve as a basis for discussion when the budgetary provisions are before us again.
The minister mentioned 76,000 cheques representing refundable portions of taxes which had not been distributed. I should like him to give us the reason for that. Is it because the addresses of the taxpayers are not now on record, or what is the reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: We have tried every method we could think of to locate thfse people.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: The minister will remember that some time earlier I asked about the relationship between his department and the Department of Public Works. I find I should have discussed that matter under this item, because it was a taxation building rather than a customs building I had in mind. I wonder if the minister has any information on the situation in St. Catharines, where I have been informed the amount of space requisitioned and provided greatly exceeds the space at present occupied by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
The explanation is that a few years ago we had a survey made by a very competent committee of outsiders, working with officials of the Department of National Revenue, in connection with the location of tax offices. At that time it was considered that it might be in the public interest to establish a tax office at St. Catharines. The department communicated with the Department of Public Works, and asked them to get us so many square feet of space. From the amount of taxes collected in a particular community we can calculate what our requirements will be. If it is decided that we need 100 square feet for each of our employees, and we have 100 employees, we shall need 10,000 or 12,000 square feet.
As things developed we found that with the great burden of work there was in connection with arrears it would not allow us to take personnel from the established offices, such as Hamilton, or Toronto, to establish a suboffice in that particular city. There were other things that entered too, such as the matter of space, and the matter of trained personnel. We shall have before us the matter of establishing a number of offices in other parts of the country. For instance, there should be an office, according to the recommendations in the report, somewhere in the north country to relieve the office in Ottawa of the amount of work it has. Primarily, though, the office should be established to give better service to the public. As I say, when we know approximately what the collections are in a district we can estimate how many people it will take to provide service. Then we can estimate the amount of floor space we shall require, and we can requisition for that. All of these things are determining factors in deciding the amount of space we need. In growing communities we feel we should make provision for the future growth of a particular district, because I think one can state without fear of contradiction that income tax collection is going to be a continuing process in this country.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following up this question, I understand that the amount of space requisitioned at St. Catharines was 16,000 square feet. Arrangements were made through public works for the leasing of that space for five years at an annual rental of $1.75 per square foot. The income tax division took occupancy of only 7,283 square feet, or less than half of the amount requisitioned and obtained by the Department of Public Works. Then I am informed that the Department of Public Works made various attempts to sublet the surplus space, and managed to rent 1,500 feet of it at a dollar per square foot or 75 cents per square foot less than they are paying. In 1949 they

sublet an additional 2,435 square feet at $1.25, or 50 cents less than the price they are paying. Up to March, 1949, or for a period of less than half the term of the lease, the Department of Public Works has experienced a direct loss of $28,000 for rental of the unoccupied space.
This brings to mind certain questions in connection with the transaction. The minister has explained why they could not occupy all the space they first wanted, but does he know whether the balance of the unoccupied space is now rented, and if so at what price?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would not know that. When we came to the conclusion we did not require all the space which we had requisitioned, and which had been leased for us, we informed public works of the amount we could release. It was up to them to re-rent it. At the present time the number of employees we have at St. Catharines is 18 or 20, and the space we are using is adequate for our needs.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: The minister has not got that information; it would only be with the Department of Public Works. I want to go back to a matter which was touched on before, the question of who pays the rent for this building. I would ask the minister what his attitude is to the suggestion that, in cases such as this, the Department of Public Works should be entitled to recover the loss from the requisitioning department, that is any loss it incurs by reason of not being able to sublet the surplus space or being able to sublet it only at prices lower than the original lease. It seems to me it would act as a control measure, not only for the Department of National Revenue but for all departments, if they were likely to be billed for such losses. I know that the money comes out of the same pocket, but I do not believe any department would like to have in its account a bill for space that was not used. I think such billing might act as a control measure on all departments, and would mean keeping their requisitioning of space to a minimum. I wonder if the minister, who is a financial man, would give his reaction to that suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL

Mr. Chairman, any comments I would make upon it would be entirely personal. I think the hon. gentleman will recognize that it has always been the policy of governments, irrespective of political shade, that all buildings are controlled by the public works department under the Public Works Act. From a strict accounting point of view, it might be better if the Post Office Department were charged rental for the buildings they occupy, and
Supply-National Revenue national revenue were charged for the space they occupy. However, that has not been the method. I presume if the government could be persuaded some time they would not be averse to a change in that direction if it were to be for the general advantage of the country.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if there is any consideration being given to the plan used in the United States, whereby when income tax returns have to be made out there is an advertisement inserted to the effect that a man will be at a certain post office in certain centres to aid the farmers and workingmen to make out their income tax returns. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-
719. To provide for advances to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, subject to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may prescribe, for working capital and to partially finance the deficit of the corporation pending determination of the provision to be made for its future financial requirements, $650,000.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
May I say at the outset, Mr. Chairman, that, contrary to the unauthorized statement of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a few minutes ago, I do not intend to make a long speech on this subject. However, even at this late stage of the session there are some points I think should be mentioned with respect to this important item.
Hon. members will recall that the special committee on radio broadcasting tabled its report in the house on June 26, two days ago. The scope of the review conducted by the committee this year was considerably narrower than that of the last two committees in the sessions of 1946 and 1947. There was a general feeling in the committee that in view of the fact that the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences is sitting and may submit its report within the next few months, it was unnecessary and perhaps undesirable for a committee of the house to cover the same ground. Consequently the whole subject of the basis and system of control of radio broadcasting in Canada was not touched upon in the committee, except briefly in relation to television. Those in competition with the corporation in local areas were not before the committee, which concentrated on an examination of the C.B.C. officials in regard to the operating side rather than the controlling and regulating side of the corporation. In a sense the evidence we heard was the evidence of only one side, in some matters; but, all things considered, I believe the committee adopted a course that was reasonable.
Before I go further I should like to pay a tribute to the officials of the corporation. The relationship between the committee and those

Supply-National Revenue officials has always been happy and harmonious, and I think every member of the committee respects the officials for the quality of their service and for their intense loyalty to the system which is placed in their hands to administer.
The report tabled in the house on June 26 contains a good deal with which some of us who did not support it nevertheless find ourselves in agreement, including the desirability of extending the services of the corporation to areas which do not enjoy those services now, and also the desirability of making improvements in the system. The report, however, was adopted by the committee on division. Those of us who were not able to support it felt on the one hand that the tone of the report was altogether too sweeping, based largely as it was on hearing only one side in certain cases. On the other hand we felt that many of the recommendations contained in the report ought to have been deferred until after the royal commission made its report. For instance, there are extensive recommendations on the subject of the financing of the operations of the system, which field is under study at the present time by the royal commission. Some of these problems have to be faced in the very near future, including the question of the basis of financing the operations of the corporation, but some of us felt that to make extensive and in many cases sweeping recommendations to the House of Commons at the present time was premature, having regard to the fact that the royal commission will be bringing in recommendations on these same matters within a short time.
When I speak of sweeping comments I would direct attention to an example of the sort of thing I mean. In the report of the committee, at page 577 of Votes and Proceedings of June 26, this statement appears in reference to what would happen if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were called upon to live within its present sources of income:
It could reduce expenditures. The consequences of doing this would, however, be disastrous.
Now, I think the word "disastrous" is too strong, as I said in the committee. Undoubtedly certain features of the system would suffer. I mention that as one example of what I think is a certain tone running through this report that goes too far, that is too sweeping.
However, sir, having regard to the desirability of economizing on time, I shall confine my remarks to three subjects which are dealt with in this report and which were considered by the committee. Those subjects

are finance, the Radio Canada building in Montreal, and television. Other subjects were considered by the committee and some of them are referred to in the report. If there were time I think those subjects are worthy of consideration in the house, but our time is very short. I shall confine myself, therefore, to those three subjects.
The subject of finance must soon be faced. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is confronted with a situation today where deficits are mounting. In the year 1948-49 the system incurred a deficit of $43,000. In the year ended March 31, 1950, a tentative figure for the deficit was given as $242,000. The officials of the corporation estimate that the deficit for the current year ending March 31, 1951, will amount to $962,000. I trust that the minister will give the committee some information concerning the way in which the particular amount in this item 719 was arrived at, because the figure of $650,000 covers only about seventy per cent of the deficit estimated by the officials of the corporation.
I have indicated that I thought in the committee, before we made recommendations on this subject, we should have the benefit of the study made by the royal commission. However, the subject is here, and I wish to make just one or two observations about it. The committee has said that it refrains from indicating how moneys should be raised, although it feels that additional money must be supplied to the corporation. In the brief tendered to the royal commission by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
-a fee of $5 was suggested for persons having receiving sets in place of the present $2.50 fee. The way in which that amount was arrived at was not made clear, except that it was shown to the committee that, while the corporation does not designate that as necessarily the method, the yield from such an increase would meet the revenue needs of the corporation for the measurable future. I wish to say this, sir, that the present licence fee of $2.50 is nothing more than a nuisance tax. The cost of collecting it has been borne, since 1947, not out of the yield of the tax to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but out of the consolidated revenue fund. The cost is running in the neighbourhood of $600,000 per year to collect this one source of revenue to the corporation. I might say that that represents about twelve per cent of the amount collected through that $2.50 licence fee, and that is an unusually heavy percentage for the cost of collecting.

In the concluding paragraph of its report the committee has drawn attention to that fact. The report reads:
Costs of collection of this licence fee run to between twelve per cent and thirteen per cent, which seems to your committee to be a very high collection cost. In saying this your committee intends no criticism of Mr. Browne or his staff,-
That is to say, the staff of the radio division of the Department of Transport.
-who in fact are both conscientious and efficient, but it would suggest that unremitting consideration be given to discovering less expensive ways of obtaining these fees.
So I say that the time is fast approaching when the house will have to face the problem of meeting the cost of operating the corporation out of a parliamentary vote.
The second subject of the three is the Radio Canada building in Montreal. That building, sir, you will recall, was acquired, by the government through the assistance of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the spring of 1948. This is the first time any parliamentary committee has had an opportunity of reviewing that purchase and the expenditure involved. The committee went to Montreal and examined the building. I was one of those who went, and I wish to say, with all frankness and emphasis, that I think that building, acquired by the government for the use of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, is a very suitable building. I was impressed by the fact that the corporation has done good work in converting the building, the former Ford hotel, to the use to which it is now to be put. The building will house not only the many services and departments of the corporation generally, but also the international shortwave service. An annex is in the course of construction now to provide for a producing centre for television in Montreal.
The price paid for the building was $2,200,000, which included a figure of $150,000 required to buy out the occupation rights of tenants then in the building. I am not in a position, and I feel that the committee was not in as good a position as members seemed to think, to pass on the price of the building. For instance, I asked in the committee whether independent appraisals or reports had been sought or obtained by the corporation from valuators before the purchase had been made. We were told that no outside valuation had been obtained by the corporation. Dr. Frigon did consult certain sources of advice open to him, and we had some evidence directed to comparing the price paid with the price paid for a nearby property acquired by the Y.W.C.A. I mention that, sir, and I do not express any opinion on the point. I should like to have seen the cor-
Supply-National Revenue poration, before making that large purchase for the government, obtain the report and advice of a competent independent valuator.
As to the cost of renovating the building and fitting it for its intended use, there are one or two facts deserving of mention. The cost of renovating the building was $1,300,000. The estimate originally prepared by the corporation was $1 million. Without inviting tenders at all, the corporation retained the services of a general contractor in Montreal, who is widely acknowledged to be a competent and efficient general contractor. He agreed to a fee not to exceed eight per cent of the corporation's estimate, that is, a maximum fee of $80,000. I have stressed the fact that no tenders were invited for the general contract. It is only fair to say that when the corporation came to let the subcontracts, about seventy per cent of the cost of the work was let to subcontractors by tender. In the case of the provision of the fittings for the building and the installation, $800,000 was the estimated amount. Again the contract was let to the same general contractor without tender. In the case of the fittings, about $345,000 of the $800,000 is being let by way of subcontract on tender.

I turn now to the third and final subject, that of television. The future of television is vast. The officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in the evidence taken, acknowledged that in television a tremendous field is opening up in this country. We are far behind the United States and the United Kingdom in this respect. It is estimated that there are 6 million television sets in use in the United States as against 5,000 in Canada.
The situation here to some extent stems from the use made of the licensing powers under the broadcasting act. With regard to television, the position under that act is precisely the same as it is with regard to sound broadcasting. The licensing of stations for the use of designated frequencies lies in the hands of the Minister of Transport, on recommendation of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
We have not any television being produced in Canada today. Any television that is being received in Canada today is being received from United States stations. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is now at work in setting up two producing centres, one in Montreal and one in Toronto. It is expected that they will be in operation by September 1, 1951. That is a long time for Canada to wait for television, Mr. Chairman.
I say that we Canadians would have had television earlier if those responsible for licensing had been willing to grant licences to persons who were making application and who were prepared to meet whatever requirements were laid down.
In previous sessions I have referred to the fact that we have not been getting television in Canada nearly as fast as we should have; and I think that those responsible for the licensing of television producing stations in Canada must accept a large share of the responsibility for this delay. In the first place, a paternalistic attitude was adopted, for which the government must take responsibility. Applicants were told, as was the radio committee, in 1947, that persons should not be permitted to risk their money in the development of television under private auspices in Canada until the experimental stage
[Mr. Maybank.j

had been passed because they might lose their money. It did not matter that they were willing to risk their money; it was felt by the government that they should not be allowed to risk it. That was not a good enough excuse.
Then a question has been raised all along, and properly raised, as to the Canadian content of television programs that might be made available if television licences were issued. Let me make it abundantly clear that I for one want to see the highest possible Canadian content in television broadcasting. Had the licensing authorities seen fit to grant licences to private applicants, it would have been the duty of the corporation, to see that a proper Canadian content appeared in all those television programs.
A third excuse given for delay was that if licences were issued to private applicants, they might just sit on their rights and not develop television. That is a pretty empty excuse when you consider that these licences would probably have been granted for a year at a time, and they are subject to close supervision on the part of the corporation. If any licensee simply sat on his rights, his licence could be immediately cancelled.
The fourth occasion for delay has been the answer given by the corporation to certain applicants, in telling competing applicants that they should get together and embark on a co-operative enterprise. There may be some difficulties presented in an area like Toronto where there are only two channels to be made available to private television stations and where there have been four principal applicants. In Montreal, on the other hand, there have not been as many private applicants as there are television frequencies available to be assigned in due course to private applicants.
I want to express the opinion that to tell people who are keen competitors in the field of sound broadcasting that their applications for television licences are not to be dealt with until they have joined together and decided to co-operate and to go into the venture as a joint enterprise, is dodging the responsibility laid by statute upon those who are charged with the duty of recommending the issuance of licences and the duty of actually issuing them.
In my opinion the explanation of this long and unfortunate delay in dealing with applications on the part of private applicants for television licences is not to be found in any of these factors that I have mentioned. They have been merely useful excuses. The fact of the matter is, sir, as I see the situation, that the government could not make up its mind

what to do about the development of television under the auspices of the publicly-owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. After a long delay they eventually made up their minds what they were to do, and the applications of others who would have liked to go ahead and develop television in this field have simply been held up in the long meantime, until the government made up their minds as to whether and how they were going to develop television through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
This long delay is most regrettable. Canadians who have shown themselves capable of keeping abreast of the world in any form of technical and scientific development have by the government's decision in fact been deprived of the development of television in Canada in these recent years, and we are now far behind the United States and the United Kingdom. I for one express here the hope that no more time will be lost in dealing with these applications.
Obviously the corporation may have a difficult problem on its hands in selecting those who are to be successful in an area like Toronto where there are more applications than there are available frequencies; but that is one of the duties laid upon the board of governors and upon the minister, and the decision is not going to be made any easier by being delayed. Therefore I urge that the time has come when some decision must be made in this field so that this development may not be longer delayed.
As I have indicated, sir, there are other matters which are worthy of the attention of the committee at this time, but in view of the fact that we are in what I understand to be the dying moments of the session, and in view of the fact that there are so many of these matters of leading importance which are to be, we expect, the subject of recommendations of the Massey commission, we may await a better opportunity to debate them at the next session of parliament, when we hope to have a full report of the royal commission before the house.

speechtext:
I have
listened to the hon. member for Eglinton speaking on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for several years now, and I feel that this was probably the least critical of his speeches. There may be a reason for that. For the first time for many years the committee got down to considering the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself, how the corporation works, what the corporation is hoping to do, and what the corporation needed. As he pointed out, the committee did a constructive job of work in its investigation, and I share with him his appreciation of the way
Supply-National Revenue in which the officials of the broadcasting corporation tendered their evidence. However, although I do think that much of what the hon. member said was constructive, there are some of his views with which I disagree, and one of them is in the field of television.
The government may have been laggard in its approach to this new avenue of education and entertainment, a matter on which I have not yet made up my mind, and one which I do not think at the moment is very important because, to use a cliche, television is still in its infancy.
The hon. member for Eglinton said we had a long time to wait for television. Well, if what I have seen in the United States is any criterion I am quite content to wait for another year or two; for much of it is not particularly edifying. What the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation must remember is this. Surveys in the United States have shown that children now are watching television for as many hours as they are receiving education in the schools. That means that television can be a tremendously important social force, either for good or for ill. My opinion, for what it is worth, is that had commercial licences been granted I doubt very much whether the owners of those licences would have realized to the full the possibilities of television; that they would have concentrated, within the rules of the system, on making as much money as possible out of their broadcasting. We would have been inundated with all sorts of commercials, and I do not share the feeling of the hon. member for Eglinton that the programs would have had a large Canadian content. I think the officials of the corporation are right when they say that television in Canada must be Canadian, must have a large Canadian content. Certainly we do not want to prohibit anything which may come from the United States or from some other country, but we have to remember first of all the responsibility of the corporation to Canada, and I do not think private interests would have fulfilled it.
There is another aspect of the situation, and it is this. Commercial groups have approached the corporation for licences for television and they have been turned down by the board of governors. They were turned down because in the opinion of the board the applicants did not make out a sufficiently good case to be awarded a licence. If the board is right, then I think there should be no criticism, and I accept the board's judgment at the moment, although my opinion of that judgment may be wrong and the hon. member for Eglinton may be right.

Supply-National Revenue
As regards the radio building, I think those of us who saw that building at Montreal were impressed by it. The corporation has every right to feel proud of its own architects and engineers who out of the shell of the Ford hotel have constructed studios which I believe will be the most up to date on the North American continent. If I have to find fault-and I have to find fault in one place-it would be with the height of some of the operating booths. Their ceilings are far too low, and on more than one occasion my head came in violent contact with beams which had not yet been hidden.
As regards finance, it is true that in the coming fiscal year the corporation may have a deficit of almost a million dollars; and yet the committee, I think unanimously, has asked the corporation to increase its expenditures for the coming year. Therefore the committee must realize that the deficit may be larger if the corporation goes ahead and gives the further services that are desired by all. Whether they can or not of course will be a matter for the corporation to decide. What is evident above all as a result of the committee's studies is the lamentable lack of money from which the corporation suffers. It must have more finances, I would say a minimum of $5 million per annum in the next two or three years, if it is going to do the job which we expect it to do. It cannot get more money from additional commercial advertising, because more advertising would be distasteful to the great majority of Canadians, and would be opposed to the policy of the corporation. The raising of the licence fee to $5 is I think impracticable. I object to the idea of the corporation having to come to parliament year after year, cap in hand, to ask for a grant of money sufficient to cover the deficits.
If we are to keep the corporation independent and as far as possible out of the political arena, then the corporation has to get money in some other way. I have a personal suggestion with which my party is not associated. The corporation should be given funds by statute on the basis of a dollar per capita of the Canadian population per annum. That would amount to about $13 million. We could then abolish the licence fees and in place of the five or six million the corporation has in the form of revenue from licence fees it would have $13 million. With that amount of money it would have no possible excuse for not giving the service the people of Canada want. I would not want my remarks to be distorted, because I feel the corporation is only too willing to give that service. However up to now it has not been able to give it because of a lack of funds. If

we want the corporation to do the job of work Canada expects it to do, then it has to be provided with money. The way I am suggesting is one which I believe will assure the independence of the corporation.

Mr. Chairman, for some time past there appears to have been grave misconception as to the value of Newfoundland as an added asset in the confederation of Canada. Many assertions have appeared in the press, credited to various people, that Newfoundland's coming into the Dominion of Canada has been a deficit. In that particular connection I should like to refer to a broadcast made, I believe, by the minister on February 17, with respect to the broadcasting facilities of the broadcasting corporation of Newfoundland, the predecessor of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation now operating in the province.
At that time the minister tabled the report of the C.B.C. and expressed some concern as to its financial position. He referred to the present financial loss and then, according to the information I have, added that the cost of the service for Newfoundland is burdensome. This is a most unfair statement. I say that because at the time of confederation the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation took over all the assets of the broadcasting corporation in Newfoundland which, at that time, consisted of a 15 kilowatt station then known as VONF, a shortwave station at St. John's, VONH, a shortwave station at Corner Brook, VOWN, a 500-watt station at Gander, VORG, as well as the equipment for the projected station they were about to open at Grand Falls, and which has since been opened.
This service included a complete and up-to-date set of transmitting equipment, a $25,000 studio building at Corner Brook, an extensive program library, and a line service between St. John's, Grand Falls and Corner Brook. In fact the broadcasting corporation of Newfoundland at that time regarded its equipment as being very much up to date. This service cost the C.B.C. not one penny. Upon the acquisition of that equipment belonging to the broadcasting corporation of Newfoundland programs were changed very considerably, and the people of that province were given what the people in the rest of Canada have come to know as soap operas. I am told 80 per cent of the broadcasting hours in each day are taken up with these soap operas. I am further informed that the improvement, if it can be called that, has not been very great.
My chief annoyance is with the suggestion that the taxpayer of Canada has been asked to carry a heavier burden. That suggestion is most unfair. Whatever burden in dollars

the Canadian taxpayer has had to assume because of the entrance of Newfoundland, Newfoundland has more than compensated for in other ways. I say that in connection with this particular operation involving the C.B.C. no additional burden has been assumed at all.
In the eleven years of operation of the broadcasting corporation in Newfoundland some facts might be of interest to the committee. It started out in 1939 with a capital investment of $8,000. Over the eleven years of its existence it was able, through the sale of licence fees, radio time and the opening of three additional stations to remodel the entire existing facilities, and to purchase all the necessary buildings which have now been handed over to the C.B.C. It was able to instal the best possible equipment and to give a service which the most severe critic could not possibly criticize.
When the broadcasting corporation of Newfoundland was dissolved as a result of having been taken over by the C.B.C. there was a surplus amounting to over $150,000. I am informed that with the revenue available to the corporation in Newfoundland it showed an annual profit of $15,000. My information is that the people of that province are very much upset about the minister's suggestion in the broadcast of February 17 to the effect that the addition of Newfoundland to the dominion has meant an additional burden upon the people of Canada generally. I feel certain that the minister would now like to retract his statement.

Item 719 in the supplementary estimates has to do with $650,000 to meet the operating deficit that is likely to occur from April 1, 1950, to April 1, 1951. We believe that will be the actual cash deficit. The amount of $962,000 that was suggested would be the paper deficit and, according to the method of accounting, known as the accrual method, would include depreciation allowances and the like.
The other item of $938,961 is made up of a revote of $638,961, which is a revote of money voted last year to finish the Radio Canada building in Montreal, plus $300,000 to meet the requirements to finish that building. ' I mention these two facts to make clear to the committee the purposes for which the money is required.
It was not my intention to discuss at length the operations of the C.B.C., because perhaps it would be out of place to do so at this time. Opportunity was given to hon.
Supply-National Revenue members to learn, from the report of the radio committee of this year, all the items having to do with the C.B.C., the international service and with television.
In his remarks about these two items the hon. member for Eglinton availed himself of the opportunity to discuss the finances of the C.B.C., Radio Canada building, and television. It is in that connection I wish to make a few remarks. I have no doubt it was made abundantly clear to the committee that the C.B.C. could not continue to operate and to produce the type of product or program they have produced throughout the year on the finances available to them, and that some method would have to be found so that they could increase their revenue. I am not in a position to say just what that method will be. As all hon. members are aware, this matter is before the Massey commission. Representatives of the C.B.C., as well as other persons throughout Canada interested in broadcasting, made representations to that commission. I feel that sometime this fall the commission will bring in a report and make suggestions to the government as to the best method of financing. Whether that will be on a fee basis or in the form of a subsidy along with fees or the total cost to be borne by the government is a matter of government policy which, of course, would be further reviewed by parliament when it meets.
I sometimes marvel that the C.B.C. has done as good a job as they have with the money made available to them. Everyone must admit that they are carrying on now with fees that were in existence ten years ago. It has been clearly demonstrated that in their operation, as in every other operation in the country, the cost of wages, services and equipment has gone up materially. It could not be expected that they would continue as they had in former years to show an operating profit. It is a good thing that they had an operating profit in former years because they were able to meet the deficit for the year ending March 1949 out of the reserves built up in former years. That obligation was not placed upon the government. The general expansion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under which the greater part of the country is now serviced is well known to all hon. members.
With reference to the Radio Canada building in Montreal, I am sure that all hon. members are familiar with that building. I was glad to hear the words of commendation from the hon. member for Winnipeg North and the hon. member for Eglinton. I am sure that they feel, as I do, that when this building is completed we shall have a radio centre second to none in the world. Within

Supply-National Revenue the last two or three weeks I have had the opportunity of visiting a number of radio centres, including the British Broadcasting Corporation in London. They have not anything such as we have. It is true that in London they propose to change from Alexandra Palace to another location, but at the present time their studios do not compare to the splendid studios we shall have in the Radio Canada building.
It is true that this has cost a lot of money. We did pay a considerable amount for the Ford Hotel building, including the purchase of the franchises which already existed. While it is not on the record that an appraisal was made of this building, I made it my personal business to interview people in Montreal who were able to give accurate information as to values and I was told that this was a good bargain at the price we paid. I am willing at any time to substantiate and back up the deal.
With reference to the transformation of the building into studios and the purchase of equipment, I am ready to admit that some of our estimates fell far short of the actual cost. In this connection I should like to give one example. A control board was needed and it took the companies that tendered something like six months to figure out their tenders and they varied all the way from $175,000, which was the figure of the Northern Electric Company, up to $375,000. When concerns in a particular business show such great variation in their estimates on a piece of equipment I think it can be readily understood why some of our estimates did not equal the actual cost. All in all it is going to take a revote of $678,000, plus an additional $300,000, to complete the building. But when the building is completed, the Canadian people will have the most outstanding broadcasting facilities in the world.
With regard to television, I cannot agree with the hon. member for Eglinton that we have been dilatory in announcing a policy or in carrying it out for the Canadian people. I remember over two years ago I went to New York and visited the studios of C.B.S., the National Broadcasting Corporation and of private concerns, and I made it my business in February to go to Chicago to see what was new there.
I found that within the last two years while there have been some advances they have not been great. In the meantime the broadcasting corporations and private industry have spent something like $50 million in an attempt to develop television. I am not ashamed to say that two years ago my advice to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation

was to delay for a time any expenditures on experimental work until we saw what advances were made in the United States. We might be accused of hanging on to their apron strings, but they had a lot more money to spend than the Canadian people, and we had no appropriation to carry out that work on behalf of the Canadian people.
Today we are able to start in with no cost at all and take advantage of the advances that have been made. Television is going to mean a lot to Canada, but it is going to cost a lot of money. As I indicated when the policy was announced, the $4,500,000 will provide only for telecasting in two languages in Montreal and in the city of Toronto. Before facilities are extended to the greater part of Canada it will cost between $10 million and $15 million.
Private industry has not been in too great a hurry to get into this business. It has been found from the experience in the United States that it costs approximately half a million dollars to set up a station, and you must be prepared to take a loss of half a million dollars before commercial advertising will place you on an earning basis. We have guarded the Canadian people against the granting of licences to people who were not prepared to go ahead. We do not want them to have the advantage of having television licences and then trafficking in them because of their increased value.
I am particularly pleased with the progress we have made. I wish to say just a word about what television will mean with regard to the electronics industry. I should like to quote an article from the Financial Post, of June 17, entitled, "TV sales climb here; export parts to U.K." It reads:
The television virus which is spreading like wildfire through the United States is gradually-infecting Canadians who are within range.
At last count (April 30):
13,500 Canadians had bought television receivers. At an average price of around $400, they had dug down for a healthy $5.4 million since Canadian General Electric turned out the first Canadian set in 1948.
That is just two years ago.
TV antennae are sprouting from more and more rooftops in the fringe areas where U.S. stations can be picked up: about 2-5 million persons in southern Ontario are within range of stations at Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, Erie, Cleveland, Toledo, Detroit; about 100,000 in the Vancouver area can get Seattle.
That means that something like 2-6 million people in this country are already within range of television stations and able to receive television programs. As at April 1 some thirteen Canadian radio manufacturers were making television receivers. So far this year they have made 5,300 sets.

Projected production for the year is 31,000 sets, with some estimates going as high as 35,000. Canadian General Electric is already producing cathode ray or picture tubes for domestic purposes, and within the last few months received an order for cathode tubes worth half a million dollars for delivery to the United States, thus giving work to Canadian people.
Some criticism has been directed toward the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for not buying their transmitters from Great Britain. We in Canada are adopting the United States standard in television. This means that United States and Canadian receiving sets will be able to record the programs coming from both United States and Canadian telecasting stations. Had we adopted the British standard, while the British machines would have been able to record the telecasts of Canadian stations, they would not have recorded those of United States stations. Therefore one order was given to Canadian General Electric and the other to RCA Victor. Canadian General Electric equipment is manufactured in the town of Peterborough, and seventy per cent of the content of that transmitter will be of Canadian manufacture. While 1 was in London I had the privilege of visiting the great factory of the Marconi wireless people in the city of Chelmsford. I went there because the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has already given them orders on a competitive basis for over $600,000 worth of equipment, thus giving Britain Canadian dollars with which to buy Canadian products.
I am not going to say anything further, except that I have carefully read the record of proceedings of the committee on radio broadcasting this year, and I want to commend the members of that committee for the very thorough manner in which the affairs of the broadcasting corporation and the international shortwave broadcasting station were reviewed. I believe the report tabled by the chairman of that committee was excellent. I must not close without mentioning the reference by the hon. member for St. John's East to the use of the word "burdensome". Perhaps that was not the right word. I meant it in the sense of an obligation, that an added obligation had been assumed, which I am sure the hon. member must recognize.

I am sorry I missed the earlier remarks of the minister, because I always listen to him with great interest. However, I have been in the railway committee room, listening to something even more enjoyable.
In view of his compliment to the committee, of which I was a member, I must say that I think this year's committee was the most useless I have ever known to be set up by this house, though no doubt it was asked

Supply-National Revenue
for by someone on this side. I made that very plain the first minute of the first day we sat. There we were, carrying on a review parallel in every particular with that which was carried on by the Massey commission dealing with the fine arts, culture and so on. I assume they included radio broadcasting under the broad term "culture"; otherwise I don't know how it could have come in through the door. I felt that we were duplicating the work of the Massey commission. I attended every sitting I could, and in the committee we were in this position: We heard only the officers of the broadcasting corporation, with the exception of a contribution made by a member of the Department of Transport, Mr. Browne, and a gentleman from Toronto whose name escapes me at the moment. So as far as the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is concerned, we had only a onesided picture.
I am not complaining. Everyone had full opportunity to come and state his views if he wished to do so. I assume that most people agreed with the idea I had, that we were pursuing a phantom and uselessly expending a great deal of time, at the same time making the job of the officers of the corporation infinitely more difficult. I did not hear the minister's remarks, and if he has answered this previously, I hope he will quickly tell me. The inquiry I make about television is this. I hear from people who should know that there are many more bands for television than for ordinary sound broadcasting. I heard the minister say that if someone starts a station he must be prepared to lose something in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars in order to get it on its feet. If someone wants to lose half a million dollars, why don't we let him do it?
We are going to have television stations in Montreal and Toronto, which will be a very satisfying business for the people who live in that neighbourhood. While a great deal of the tax money comes from that area, ultimately the rest of us are going to be paying for television for those people. We in the distant points hope that some day we shall have the privilege of buying a television set and enjoying it. What I am utterly unable to understand is this. If a person in the city of Edmonton wants to lose his money in an effort to give that area television, why in the world is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, who admittedly are doing nothing in that area and do not intend to do anything for some time to come, prohibiting the establishment of that station? Why is it the policy of the government-because it is the government which issues the licence-not to permit 
someone to attempt to make television go in these outlying places?
I know all the arguments in favour of Canadian culture, and I know that we are going to have Canadian programs. I trust some day you will find someone to listen to them; that is at least a hope I express. I want to pay a compliment to our committee chairman this year. He had nothing very difficult to do, but he is one of those fellows who can do a pleasant thing in a very difficult way. There is no doubt about that; the word "carried" came in and you did not even have to press a button. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend, at this stage of the session, to launch into a discussion on the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. However, as the mining industry ranks third, in our country, both in production and exports, I believe it well deserves a few minutes of our time.
There are several mines within the limits of the constituency of Villeneuve and it behooves me, I believe, as the member for that constituency, to draw the attention of my hon. friends to certain facts and to quote certain figures which may help them to understand the true importance of this industry.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, when we look at the country's record for the first half of the century, we realize what mining has done in transforming the economic and social life of the country. If our country is a leading power in the complex world of today, it is due to the

great expansion of its mining industry. Canada leads all other countries in the production of asbestos, nickel, platinum and its associated metals; Canada is second in zinc and cadmium, third in gold, copper, magnesium and cobalt, and fourth in silver and lead. We have reason to be proud of our country's record in mineral production during the second world war, when the allied nations were so pressed by an urgent need for base metals.
During the six war years, the total value of our mineral production amounted to over $4 billion. Of this, $1 billion worth of base metals only was contributed to the war effort, including 3-6 billion pounds of copper, 1-26 billion pounds of nickel, 1-6 billion pounds of zinc, and 1-3 billion pounds of lead. That is a fair record for a country like Canada. It is true to say that we surprised ourselves with the vastness of our own war contribution.
In time of peace we are continuing to produce minerals at an accelerated pace. The total Canadian mineral production for the year 1945 amounted to $499 million; in 1947 it amounted to $645 million; and in 1949 to the spectacular figure of $890-2 million. This last figure includes the production of Newfoundland, which amounted to $25-7 million. These are impressive figures if we consider that the total mineral production in Canada during the year 1900 barely exceeded $64 million.
According to the most recent survey the production of 1949 is divided as follows: Metallic metals, $534-8 million, including gold to an amount of $147-8 million; nonmetallic metals-that is fuels-$184-2 million; other non-metallic metals, including asbestos, barite, salt and quartz, $62-3 million; clay products and other structural materials, $108-8 million.
The mining industry is the third leading producer in Canada. Not long ago we could read in the Financial Post, immediately before the trade fair took place in Toronto, this title: "Canada: The largest per capita trading nation in the world". Below that we could also read:
In the past thirty years we've seen $80 billion of goods and merchandise cross our borders.
Our total export in 1949 amounted to $3 billion and the leaders in the commodities which were exported were the following: wood, wood products and paper to the amount of $875-3 million; agricultural and vegetable products, $773 million; non-ferrous metals, $426-6 million. The world today has become dependent upon Canada for such necessities as nickel and asbestos. Without our mines humanity would be sadly deficient in gold, 55946-273
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys silver, copper, zinc, lead and platinum. Canadian uranium played a vital role in the development of atomic energy. In metals, above all, Canada outdid itself not only in quantity but in quality and diversity. As countries go, Canada is still young.
The foregoing is a short resume of its achievement in mineral production. It is, we can say, our duty to keep up the pace.
Here I should like to refer hon. members to an article which appeared in Saturday Night of June 27. I should like to read these few lines:
Prospects for the sale of Canadian metals in the United States never have been as promising as they are today. ... In the 12 months ending February 28.	1938, the United States imported
$43 million worth of non-ferrous metals from Canada. For the 12 months ending February 28, 1950, they had jumped to $198,800,000.
These are impressive figures. In another paragraph we can read the following;
The U.S. has less than a 35-year supply of 21 out of 35 minerals. Some of these, such as petroleum, copper, lead and zinc, are minerals in which the United States led the world for many years.
While the U.S. has lost her leadership in the raw materials field, Canada is fast becoming the world's greatest source of such items as copper, zinc, lead, nickel, and aluminum. Tomorrow she may take her place as one of the leading producers of iron ore, petroleum and titanium.
Non-ferrous ores and metals constitute the largest single classification of imports to the United States. Ores and metals were brought into the States to the tune of approximately $550 million in 1947: $775 million in 1948, and $840 million in 1949. And such shipments bid fair to be much higher again this year.
After taking cognizance of this article we can see that in the United States we have a big market for our metal production, and it is up to us either to increase our production or to find new mines.
Here I should like to say this. If our country is a leader today in base metal production and if we are capable of such achievements in mining during the first part of the century, I will venture to say that it is owing to the incentive our prospectors had when they were prospecting, always hoping to find that famous gold mine.
Today many people think that the gold mines are not so important. But I will say this; it is owing to the fact of the prospectors looking for gold mines that our base metal mines were found. We must not forget that fact. Besides that, the production of gold during the last three years has been increasing, owing to the encouragement on the part of the government. The gold production in Canada from 1858 to 1949 amounted to $3.3 billion. The gold production in 1945 amounted to $103.8 million; in 1946, to $104 million; in 1947, to $107.5 million; in 1948, to $125.6 million and in 1949 to $147.7 million. We
4324	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys see that there was a substantial increase from 1947 to 1949. We know that it is mostly due to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which we call EGMA as an abbreviation.
Hon. members are aware that this act will terminate at the end of December, 1950. I will not ask the minister to state definitely what the government intends to do after that date, but I will urge him to study closely all that is related to the gold mines. For instance, we know that some gold mines do not need this emergency assistance; on the other hand, we know that other gold mines need it. The word "emergency" was correct when the government passed that act and it_ is still correct today in the case of many mines. If the low-grade mines today did not have this act to help them, and did not have this bonus, they would certainly be obliged to close. That would be a bad thing. It would have a very bad effect on many parts of the country from British Columbia to the maritimes. I shall cite only a few instances in my own constituency and especially in my own town where we have four gold producers and they are all low-grade mines.

We know that our prospectors will go into the bush and try to find a gold mine but they will not go into the bush and try to find a base metal mine. It has been proved in the past in all the mining districts of Canada that wherever the prospectors went to find gold mines they also found base metal mines, and our base metal mines are leaders in our mining industry.

Hon. members may feel that Newfoundland is getting a lot of prominence in the discussion of these estimates, but it is because it is the expiry of the first full year of union.
The report of the Department of Mines and Resources which I have in my hand deals with the fiscal year ended March 31, 1949, and it is very difficult to know exactly what was done in Newfoundland during the past summer. In reading the report I notice that a great deal of investigation has been going on in different places on geological, hydrographic, topographic and engineering work. I am wondering whether we have to wait until next year before we get any indication of any discoveries that were made in Newfoundland.
In connection with these reports, I also notice that the department is assisting industry to a very large extent, making studies of minerals, and helping in the search for minerals. In Newfoundland, as hon. members know, we have three mines, the iron ore mine on Bell island, the lead zinc nickel composite ore at Buchans and the fluor spar mine at St. Lawrence in the southern part of Newfoundland. In addition to that the country is highly mineralized. In the past we have suffered from lack of trained geologists. We have only one geologist at work in the island. Before he was appointed we had to engage a man from Princeton, Professor Snelgrove.
Great work was done in the early days by Mr. Howley, but nothing compared to what is going on in the other provinces of Canada. I am wondering whether the minister has considered extending the services which have been given to other provinces in regard to these minerals, which are considered the most profitable at the present time.
We have an oil well at Parson's Pond, which was discovered over a hundred years ago, but we do not know the extent of it, and we cannot know it without proper geological and more intensive surveys. I do not know what facilities the department has for estimating what quantity is there but I understand that the provincial government is engaging the services of an airborne magnetometer for this summer. With regard to radioactive investigation, I saw in one of the local papers that a discovery of radioactive minerals had been made down there. I am wondering if that has been brought to the attention of the minister's department? Finally, what relationship is there between this Department of 55946-273J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys Mines and Technical Surveys and the department of resources in Newfoundland?

There is no relationship

With respect to the work going on in Newfoundland, or that contemplated this summer, one engineer will be there to make a general investigation of the mineral resources of the province. At the same time he will act as deputy inspector of explosives. A ceramics engineer will investigate the clay deposits and will assist the brick industry. A third engineer will make a survey of peat bogs for the provincial department of agriculture, and will also investigate the suitability of peat for fuel purposes.
We intend to put out a number of parties. In connection with the geological survey we will have four field parties. In topographical survey we will have five field parties, and three in the Quebec-Labrador section. In the hydrographic surveys we will have three boats charting Newfoundland waters; in the geodetic survey we will have four field parties, and five in Labrador. In the legal survey we will have one field party on radar altimeter work. In the geographic branch we will have two field parties in Labrador and two in Newfoundland. In connection with the dominion observatory there will be one party on magnetic surveys work, and there will be aerial photography of 14,183 square miles of Newfoundland done by the Spartan company and 800 square miles of Labrador done by the R.C.A.F.
I suggest that contemplates a very good program for the first years in which we have undertaken to do work in that province. The party is made up in some instances of an engineer and four or five other people. Parties can be either larger or smaller than that. So that in all these different branches of the Mines and Technical Surveys department, including geological, topographical, hydrographic and so on, we are detailing to Newfoundland a very fair proportion of the available staff for this kind of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys; Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
This vote provides for office, laboratory and field investigations relating to metallic minerals, industrial minerals, fuels, and mineral economics. The Geology and Mines Act of 1907 provided that the mines branch of the then department of mines was "to make such chemical, mechanical and metallurgical investigations as are found expedient to aid the mining and metallurgical industry of Canada." The present mines branch assists the bringing into production of Canadian mineral deposits by developing suitable ore-dressing and bene-ficiation methods. Research is being carried
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys out to find efficient processes for treating low-grade and complex ores and to find means of lowering the costs of producing such metals as lithium and titanium.
The facilities in physical metallurgy are used to assist Canadian industrial development, and major problems in research concern advice and assistance to the national research council in connection with the atomic energy project. Co-operation with the Department of National Defence and with manufacturers of equipment involves various fields of research on alloy metals, including testing and development to find metals most suitable for service at extreme low temperatures and other metals which will withstand the extremely high temperatures required for jet propulsion. The branch, at the request of national research council, has undertaken investigations into the application of radioactive tracer materials for industrial and scientific problems. Some of the problems involve work of highly confidential or secret nature. In the field of fuels, close liaison is maintained with the dominion coal board, and major projects on coal include evaluation of Canadian coals for stoker operation and research on pressurized combustion to develop the use of coal in turbine propulsion. The problems in coal, natural gas and oil technology referred to the branch are many and varied. Included in the investigations and experimental work is the means of extracting and utilizing the oil in the bituminous sands of Alberta.
The hon. member's question referred more particularly to Nova Scotia, but the principles I have enunciated would apply to that province as they apply to other parts of Canada.

speechtext:
This appropriation is to
maintain the services of the radioactivity division of the bureau of mines. These services were commenced in 1945 at the request of the minister of munitions and supply and the president of the national research council for the purpose of carrying on research on ore dressing and recovery of uranium from ores from the crown-acquired Eldorado mine at Great Bear Lake. The services to the crown company, Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited, are increasing in importance with the understanding of large-scale experimental work on the problem of recovering uranium lost by present methods of treatment. The policies of the atomic energy control board, in stimulating search in Canada for uranium-bearing minerals, are having widespread effect in causing new discoveries and the board takes the view, for security reasons concerning processes, that the burden of assaying and carrying on development of ore treatment methods for privately controlled uranium enterprises should be borne by the mines branch. The work of the section is part of the secret atomic energy project being carried out by certain government departments. Included in the activities is research into methods of detecting uranium which may have an important bearing upon the results of future prospecting in Canada.
The development of uranium ores, as I am sure the hon. gentleman knows, has been stimulated greatly by the increased price for uranium oxide. At the moment I believe it is somewhere in 'the neighbourhood of $6.00 per pound as compared with $2.75 per pound about a year ago. There has been a lot of activity in that particular development. The government, through Eldorado Mining and Refining Company, is in the market for uranium oxide as it is produced. The department of mines attempts to assist people by
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys giving them such information as is available concerning the places where uranium might be found, taking into consideration geological factors. The department gives information with regard to the type of instruments which are now being used for the detection of those ores.

This vote of $1,524,774 is to continue the geological survey of all the provinces of Canada, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, with the object of determining potential sources of minerals, oil and gas; to initiate and maintain research facilities in all the branches of geology, with the object of advancing the practical application of geology to the search for mineral resources; to compile records and issue maps of field investigations and studies for the purpose of informing and assisting prospectors, mining men and others interested.

This has to do with the gratuity which is paid to the widow of Dr. Feniak, who was an employee on the geological survey of Canada. He lost his life while on duty in the Northwest Territories.
Under the workmen's compensation ordinance, Yukon Territory, Mrs. Feniak received a lump sum payment of $5,000 for herself and $1,500 for her two children, a total of $6,500. Had hqr claim been administered by the Ontario workmen's compensation board she would have been provided with a pension of

$50 per month until death or remarriage plus $10 per month for each of her two children until they reach the age of sixteen years. It is obvious that the Ontario pension offers greater security over the years and takes into account the age of the children. The income from her present lump sum benefit will be most inadequate for herself and the two children in the years directly ahead. Mrs. Feniak is but thirty years of age.
Mrs. Feniak's case was brought to the attention of the Northwest Territories council with a view to having the compensation paid to her supplemented by ordinance or otherwise. The council were in favour of assisting her in this way and sought the opinion of the deputy minister of justice as to whether they had the authority to do so. However, the deputy minister of justice gave an opinion that they did not have this authority.
Since Dr. Feniak's widow and children are to suffer financially, because of the geographical location of his work at the time of death, this department considers that a gratuity of $2,000 would be of some assistance to Mrs. Feniak in bringing up her two small children.
That is why this is sought as a vote from parliament.
