An explanation of this is, to authorize and provide for a compassionate payment, by way of reimbursement to the province of Manitoba, of the department's share of the cost in connection with an accident to Angus Thomas, employed by the Ontario-Manitoba boundary commission, who 55946-274J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys was severely burned while engaged in survey work in northern Manitoba.
Angus Thomas, an Indian dog driver employed by the Ontario-Manitoba boundary commission, was severely burned in a tent fire on January 25, 1948, while engaged in survey work in northern Manitoba. His injuries have rendered him totally disabled. The commission filed a claim on his behalf with the workmen's compensation board of Manitoba. This claim was accepted and it was necessary for some time to pass before the full extent of the medical and pension costs could be determined.
The Ontario-Manitoba boundary commission is financed jointly by the federal, Ontario and Manitoba governments, each government being responsible for one-third of the cost. Because they are closer to the work being done, the department of mines and natural resources of the Manitoba government handles the accounts for the commission. Commission expenditures are made through the open ledger account of the Manitoba government who in turn are reimbursed by the other governments.
During the winter of 1950 this department was informed by the workmen's compensation board of Manitoba of the cost incident to the accident sustained by Thomas, as well as an estimate of the future cost. Payments made by the workmen's compensation board of Manitoba up to January 21, 1950, amount to $1,470.82 plus medical expenses, making a total of $4,520.70.
In addition the board have on hand an outstanding air transportation account of Central Northern Airways Limited in the amount of $172.20. I could give considerable detail, but perhaps it would be sufficient to say that the gist of the whole matter is that the sum of $7,000 comprises $6,836.85 for the reimbursement of the province of Manitoba in connection with Thomas' medical costs to date and his compensation pension to date and in future, and the remainder is to provide for the possible medical and transportation expenses which may be incurred during the year 1950-51.

During my years in parliament going back for the past fifteen years the development of Abasand oils has been a live issue. Money was appropriated for it; but during the last two or three years, since the enormous development of the Alberta oil fields, not so much attention has been paid to the Abasand development.
The department has taken an interest since early in this century in investigating the occurrence and possible utilization of these sands as a source of petroleum products. A scarcity of petroleum during world war II stimulated investigation of these deposits and of the recovery of bitumen.
In 1942 drilling was undertaken to discover, if possible, a uniformly rich deposit of the sands which could support a large oil industry. By 1947 a four and a half square mile area had been located containing an estimated 900 million barrels of bitumen.
In 1943 the government, in an effort to solve other problems confronting the utilization of bituminous sands, undertook to finance the improvement of the plant of Abasand Oils Limited. Some results were obtained but the separation plant was destroyed by fire on June 16, 1945.
Because of the change in the war picture by that time, the federal government decided not to continue with the project, and an agreement was entered into between the federal government and Abasand Oils, conveying to the latter all rights and equipment, on consideration of which the company undertook to pay the government the sum of $2,063,289.11, part of it to be reimbursed from the sale of movables; another part from the proceeds of rentals on buildings and machinery; the major portion, amounting to $1,913,427.08, to be reimbursable at the rate of 5 cents per barrel of bitumen produced or contained in materials sold, if and when the company would enter into production.
The indebtedness of the company to the federal government now stands at $1,802,107.39.
The department's view is that the production of petroleum products from the bituminous sands would be uneconomic in competition with Alberta crudes at their present prices.
The mines branch have developed on a pilot plant scale a cold water method for the separation of bitumen from the bituminous sands.

Item agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, there is a matter connected with the Department of Fisheries which I believe I might well discuss under this item,. I feel sure however that the people in my section of the Pacific coast, irrespective of their political persuasions, would never forgive me if I were to undertake to speak on this, subject without first expressing their appreciation to the department and its minister.
I would not like to say that they have no complaints and no requests for betterment. No one in this parliament knows better than the Minister of Fisheries that in any business once anyone reaches a stage of complete satisfaction and complacency, once he stops trying to improve and to get ahead, just at that time he begins to slip back. So I shall warn the minister that we will never stop asking for more, and expecting to get it.
I wish to tell him however that that part of the fishing industry for which I am speaking, along the northern Pacific coast of British Columbia, is appreciative indeed of the work being done in their interests and for their good by the Department of Fisheries. They place the credit for that largely where it rightfully belongs, namely with the Minister of Fisheries.
The subject I wish to discuss this evening is that of the halibut season on the Pacific coast. Perhaps I shall suggest certain changes in the powers and set-up of the international fisheries commission. May I make it clear however that I am not attacking the members of that commission. On the contrary I am convinced that they are doing as good a job as is possible under present conditions, and that they are not only keen but also enthusiastic in their work, which is being done most conscientiously and efficiently.
They are restricted by a convention and a statute. I wish to discuss the convention and the statute. The views I am about to discuss this evening are those I obtained before this session opened from an open mass meeting of the fishermen in my area held under the auspices of the deep-sea fishermen's union, with the approval of the halibut vessel owners association, and from conversations with several sound and experienced halibut fishermen.
The statements of fact I am going to make were acquired in that way. I believe they are correct. If not the minister will correct me. If I make any misstatement of fact it will be through error and not by intent. The administration of the Pacific coast halibut fisheries, so far as the closed season is concerned, comes under a convention between

the United States and Canada signed on June 29, 1937, and confirmed by chapter 36 of the statutes of that year. That convention gives to the international fisheries commission the power to make certain recommendations. I wish to emphasize the fact that they have power to recommend, not to order. The commission does not make final orders, and it does no enforcing. The operative words there are these:
The international fisheries commission . . . subject to the approval of the President of the United States of America and of the Governor General of Canada-
Then it goes on to set out the powers to divide the waters into fishing areas, to limit the catch, to set a closed season, to fix the size and character of the appliances, and so forth. I wish to emphasize the words, "subject to the approval of the President of the United States of America and of the Governor General of Canada" which surely prove that when the orders are finally issued they are government orders. That point is made clear in the statute itself. I quote section 9, subsection 1, which reads:
The governor in council may make orders and regulations to give effect to any permission, limitation, regulation, prohibition, or other action of the international fisheries commission, pursuant to the provisions of the convention.
I wish to establish, first, that the powers of the commission are to make recommendations, and, second, that the orders as finally issued are orders of the respective governments. The next point I want to make is that the powers of the commission are based! upon principles of conservation only. The commission is set up in the interests of the conservation of the north Pacific halibut fishery. The commission is not set up to regulate the industry. Under the terms of reference they cannot be influenced in their judgment by matters of business practice. As I say, they are restricted to the title of the treaty, which is, "for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the northern Pacific ocean and Bering sea". Such recommendations as they see fit to make can be made only in that connection.
But the government and) we in this parliament are interested, not only in conservation but in. the efficient conduct of the industry. We are interested/ further in the working conditions of the men engaged in the industry. I can hardly say their comfort and convenience, because those words are a little soft when applied to an industry of that sort, but efficiency and satisfaction in their work are matters that can be considered in connection with any industry, including the fishing industry.
Supply-Fisheries
As I say, my second point is that the commission is confined in its recommendations to those concerning conservation, but the government of the country can take into consideration matters having to do with the most efficient conduct of the north Pacific halibut fishery.
What the halibut fishermen want is a split season, or two seasons. The present halibut season is too short. I think it is necessary that one should explain how it comes about that there is a restricted halibut season and how such season is based on principles of conservation. The commission has power to investigate and to recommend what quantity of fish it is safe from a conservation point of view to take from any given area.
Let us say that they take a given area and say that 10 million pounds of halibut can safely be taken from that area. When those 10 million pounds are taken the season comes to an end. The claim of the halibut fishermen is that the present season is too short for efficient operation. It is possible that there are other views; it is possible that other branches of the fishing industry on the Pacific coast may not be in favour of changing the present short halibut season. I have no idea what the views of the large companies are, but I suspect that the salmon fishermen like the present short halibut season very much because it enables them to fish for halibut for a few weeks andi then go into their own line of salmon fishing.
The halibut fisherman, with the type of craft he uses, cannot go into salmon fishing, and from his view a certain proportion of those engaged in salmon fishing chisel into his industry. I admit that there may be different views on this matter but I suggest to the government and the minister that the views of the producers of halibut should receive first consideration. It is their industry that is primarily involved, and their views should receive paramount consideration. In justification of my statement that the season is too short, may I point out that in area No. 2 in 1931 the halibut season was 245 days. It has steadily shrunk until in 1949 it was 34 days, and this year it was 31 days. In area No. 3 the season was 245 days in 1931, and in 1949 it had shrunk to 73 days.
Thirty-one or 34 days is a pretty short period in which to earn the most of your year's income. I do not think that is an unfair statement to make. The halibut fishermen are so equipped that they cannot fish for any other type of fish. If a ship has a slight mechanical break-down and loses a trip, or even three or four days, that constitutes a substantial part of its annual earning capacity. Halibut vessels cost a lot of

Supply-Fisheries
money, and they can be paid tor only by earnings. Thirty-one or 34 days is a short time in which to earn an amortized share of the cost of a halibut vessel.
Recently 'there has been an unfortunate slump in dogfish livers, which used to be a first-class sideline. That alternative to which the halibut men could turn is being restricted also. I may be wrong in my next statement, but it occurs to me that this progressive curtailing of the season may result eventually in forcing up the price to a point where it will be beyond the reach of the average consumer.
I said that there might be opposing views to my other suggestions, but I do not think there are any opposing views to my next suggestion, which is based on conservation. The halibut season for this year opened on May 1 and closed on June 1. There are halibut on the banks in July. It is the opinion of the fishermen on the coast that those halibut which are on the banks in July were not there in May and will not be there next May, and so are not being fished at all. In other words there is a run of fish not being considered, which does not come into the picture when the quotas are being fixed. In that connection I want to read the binding words dealing with the season, as they appear in the treaty. It is within the power of the commission to-
(c) prohibit departure of vessels from any port or place, or from any receiving vessel or station, to any area for halibut fishing, after any date when in the judgment of the international fisheries commission the vessels which have departed for that area prior to that date or which are known to be fishing in that area shall suffice to catch the limit which shall have been set for that area. . . .
So if a limit of ten million pounds is set for an area and that limit is caught every year by the first week in June, those July fish are not caught at all. I understand that scientific opinion is gradually coming to be the same as -that of the fishermen themselves, that these July or later runs are not being fished. In that connection I note with pleasure further down the page that item No. 118 is being increased by $15,000. I presume the United States government will have to match that, since the expenses of this commission are borne fifty-fifty. May I express the hope that the $30,000 so made available, or some portion of it, will be used, as I have reason to believe it will, in proving or disproving our theory that those July and later halibut are never fished. If that theory can be proved correct, there are two to four million pounds or more of halibut available to be caught every year which at present are not being touched, which presumably die a natural death and represent a total waste. Therefore
IMr. Applewhaite.l
I claim, and with reason, that if our arguments are correct the opening of a later season can have no possible adverse effects from the conservation angle.
To get at those July or later fish would involve a split season. The fishermen on the coast are of the opinion that the Canadian and United States governments do not interpret the present treaty in the same way. I have no personal knowledge of the interpretation either government places upon the law, but I must read this section once more in order to explain to the committee the problem with which the fishermen are faced. The powers of the commission in connection with fixing the season, skipping some words, are:
-to prohibit departure of vessels from any port or place . . . after any date when in the judgment of the international fisheries commission the vessels which have departed . . . shall suffice to catch the limit . . . set for that area.
Under a very strict interpretation of those words there might be power to prohibit vessels sailing into a ten million pound area after eight million pounds had been accounted for in order to permit them to return later in the year and pick up the other two million pounds. A very close reading of the provision, however, might lead one to the opinion that the fishermen may only continue fishing until the limit has been caught, and then they must stop for that year. The fishermen on the Pacific coast are of the opinion that this is not the interpretation placed upon the treaty by the Canadian government, that the Canadian government believe that under the present treaty there may be power to order a split season. They also believe that the United States government holds a different view. Rightly or wrongly my fishermen are firm in their belief that the view of the United States government is that under the present treaty there shall be one season only. I do not know what the interpretation is; but if we are right in believing that the Canadian government thinks the power is there now, then we respectfully suggest that the government could not have much objection to entering into a new treaty which would state in so many words that the right is there, putting the matter beyond all possible question.
So our request is that this government, at the earliest possible moment, enter into negotiations with the United States with a view to drafting a new treaty to cover this point. A draft has been drawn already, of which I have a copy. I understand the author is Dr. Chapman, special assistant to the under secretary of state of the United States. At any rate I know Dr. Chapman read and

explained this treaty at public hearings for fishermen on the Pacific coast. On the point I have been discussing the new treaty would read as follows:
-the international fisheries commission, with the approval of the president of the United States of America and of the governor general of Canada, may, after investigation has shown such action to be necessary, in respect of the nationals, inhabitants and fishing vessels and boats of the United States of America and of Canada, and in respect of halibut or sablefish or both, as the case may be:
(a)	divide the convention waters into areas;
(b)	establish one or more open or closed seasons, annually, as to each area.
We have been given to understand in some quarters that objection has been raised to extending these powers, to giving the international fisheries commission too much power. I repeat that under this draft, as under the existing treaty, the powers of the international fisheries commission in reference to enforcing their regulations are entirely subject in Canada to the governor general in council and in the United States to the similar organization under the president. Incidentally this draft treaty also makes another change; it increases the number of members of the international fisheries commission from four to six. This would enable one of the United States members to be a representative of Alaska; and I should mention that under my hand I have a copy of a resolution from the associated boards of trade of central British Columbia, passed last year, endorsing that principle.	.
I am not wedded to the terms of this draft treaty, but I am wedded to its objectives. I do not plead for the government to sponsor this particular draft, but I do plead with them to investigate the possibility of negotiating some document which will incorporate the main provisions of this draft. The draft to which I refer has been adopted by the united fishermen and allied workers union in a statement I have under my hand. It has been approved by the united fishermen's cooperative association, which approval I also have.
What about the industry as a whole; what is their view? A poll has been taken up and down the Pacific coast among both boat owners and fishermen. It is not unanimous, which proves that it is genuine. I should like to give the committee the result of that poll. In Juneau, Alaska, both boat owners and fishermen were against adopting the split season. In Petersburg, Alaska, the boat owners were against adopting the split season and the fishermen expressed no opinion. In Ketchikan, Alaska, owners and fishermen were both in favour of a split season. In
Supply-Fisheries
Prince Rupert, British Columbia, owners and fishermen were both in favour of a split season. In Vancouver owners and fishermen were both in favour of a split season. In Seattle, Washington, owners and fishermen both favoured a split season. I do not think there can be much doubt, therefore, as to how the industry feels on this question.
In conclusion, therefore, I should like to urge this government to give prompt and favourable consideration to these proposals which have the overwhelming support of the people who are concerned, the halibut fishermen on the Pacific coast. I would ask them to bear in mind, if it is true that they feel the power is there and so a change is not necessary, that it cannot do any harm to make the power even more obvious. I should like to ask the government to bear in mind what we realize, that the whole treaty system is set up on a basis of conservation. My fishermen want a split season, but they do not want to affect in any way the excellent conservation work that is being done. On the contrary they feel the adoption of their proposals would assist in conserving the stocks which at the present time are being fished, and at the same time make available a stock that has never been fished.
I would ask the government to consider that it is the long line fisherman himself who wants it. It is for him I am speaking in making this proposal. I would ask the government to consider, although it has nothing to do with conservation, the benefits that would be derived by enabling men engaged in the halibut fishing industry to know that if they come into port on Saturday and stay over until Monday they have not lost one-tenth of the year. That may sound exaggerated to some members, but it is equivalent to a little over a month of our time. I have seen a ship held up for thirty-six hours and thus miss a trip, and that represented about one-sixth of her earning capacity for the year. The only other objection that I think might be raised at this time is that the argument that the July run is not being fished may not be sound. It may be that those July fish on the banks were the same ones that were not caught in May. Well, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that if that is true the commission will not recommend a split season. It would not hurt anyone, since international negotiations take a long time, to make the necessary treaty provisions so that, if the scientists and conservationists believe it is justified, we will be ready for the next season. Then we shall not have the men who are trying to make a living starting their year's work on the first

of May, finishing it on the first of June, and wondering how they are going to get by the rest of the time.

It may not be correct, but the understanding of the men who interviewed me was that the Canadian government had been delaying action. Mr. Chairman, I just want to speak briefly about a problem that is confronting the fishermen on the Atlantic coast. This problem is connected with the sardine industry. The fishermen on the east coast today are facing a season that is not so bright, owing to the fact that the prices paid for raw materials by the Maine canners have been cut in two since the first day of June. The demand for sardines is very limited. Other branches of the fishing industry on the east coast are faced with the same problem. At the present time, one of our very important industries in the Quoddy area is the pollock fishery. These fishermen are in a position to make very large catches 'of fish, but the price has dropped from ten to twelve cents each during the past few weeks.
[Mr. Applewhaite.l
In my opinion the most serious problem is presented by the sardine industry. At the present time the cost of maintaining and operating sardine weirs is at the highest peak in the history of this country. Fishermen who had a few thousand dollars this spring decided, owing to the fact that during the past eight or nine months the catch of sardines had been limited, and it was assumed the market was clear, to take their savings to buy the materials to go back into the business this year. Up until the first of June the catch had been very small. Then sardines struck in large quantities in Maine and Charlotte county and also in Saint John county. The fishermen were able to shut off thousands of hogsheads of sardines in coves. In a very short time it was found that there was no market, and the price dropped from $20 a hogshead to $10 in a few days. Along the main coast, where there were thousands of hogsheads shut off the fishermen held them until the situation was hopeless, then lifted the twine and let them swim away. Today the demand is limited and the price is 50 per cent lower than it was one month ago.
Listening to the debates in this House of Commons, I often wonder just what would happen if the price of wheat dropped 50 per cent or the price of beef suddenly dropped 50 per cent, or any other of the primary products. We would see the members from all the agricultural districts in Canada telling their story in the House of Commons. This problem is one which seems to have created very little interest, and very little worry except to the people who are directly affected. I do hope that conditions may improve, but I can assure you that at the present time the outlook is gloomy.
One week ago tonight I attended a meeting in my home town. It was an international gathering and there were 50 or 60 representatives from the state of Maine. A large proportion of that number were engaged in the sardine canning industry. Mr. Pike, who is president of the Maine sardine canners association, spoke at that meeting and gave us a clear picture of the situation in which the fishermen and canners find themselves today. Markets are extremely dull. They were hesitant as to buying sardines at the price they had been paying for two or three years, holding off when it looked as if the price of canned sardines would drop. For that reason about 50 per cent of the canneries in the state of Maine are operating. The other 50 per cent have their doors still closed and it is doubtful as to when they will start again.
During the war a ceiling price was put on sardines. The fishermen were given to

understand that after the war every effort would be made to maintain a fair price in order to make up for some of the loss they sustained during the war when they might have taken, on many occasions, double what they were getting. But it has not worked out just that way, and they find themselves in the same position they have found themselves in after every war. The market is limited; the price has been cut in two; and the outlook is none too good. I hope that the Canadian canneries will continue to pay $15 per hogshead as they are at the present time. They are taking perhaps 50 per cent of the sardines that are being caught. In Saint John county and in Charlotte county there are hundreds of hogsheads for which markets cannot be found.
I intend to speak only briefly because I realize that we are trying to get through. But before taking my seat I want to compliment the Minister of Fisheries and the officials of his department for the concerted effort they have made during the past few years to create a more friendly feeling and greater evidence of co-operation between the fisheries department and those engaged in the fishing industry. It is quite noticeable where I live that every effort has been made by the fisheries department to create this friendly feeling; and I know that between the industry and the department there is better co-operation today than there has been at any previous time.
I believe that if those engaged in the fishing industry and also those in the canning industry can be educated to provide a better article, it will do the industry a great deal of good. In the past our weakness to a great extent has been that we were not providing as good an article as we could provide. I believe that the Department of Fisheries, through their efforts, and with the knowledge they have, can be of great assistance to the industry. I want to say that the assistance they are giving and the evidence of co-operation between the department and the industry are greatly appreciated. If it continues, I believe that we may look forward to something better in the fishing industry in the future.

I wish to join with the hon. member for Skeena on the other side of this great country and on the other side of this chamber in extending to the minister, as I have before, and all those associated with him, our thanks for his work and for the statement of the work that he is doing. I expect he is going to hear continually from this side of the chamber requests such as he heard from the district represented by the hon. member for Skeena.
Supply-Fisheries
As hon. members of the committee are aware, I have been asking questions on various occasions about this matter of the fisheries, particularly as it pertains to Newfoundland. I do that not for the sake of talking but because I realize, as do hon. members and as does the minister, how vital this industry is to Newfoundland itself. When I talk of the fishery, I refer particularly- and I intend to do so tonight-to the salt codfish industry. In order that hon. members may be able to evaluate the position in the proper perspective I should like to say that the total production of all the provinces engaged in the salt codfishing industry is scarcely 40 per cent of the average normal Newfoundland production. The hon. member for Charlotte will probably know that as well. Moreover, the markets to which salt codfish is sold by the other provinces are all on this side of the Atlantic. Because of the size of the catch of the other provinces and its relation to the total industry of each of the mainland provinces the salt fish trade is of comparatively little importance to these provinces.
The question of marketing of any surplus occasions little worry and the only problem really is the sale of the current year's catch. The problem in the newest province is quite different indeed, because almost half the catch each year must be sold in European markets. If prices are low or if there is difficulty in making sale, the effect on the economy of the province might well be ruinous. It must be remembered that salt fish supports practically half the total economy of the province of Newfoundland. Up to the present time there is no alternative means of providing earning power and I suggest that it is much better to produce salt fish, even though government assistance may be required, than to stop fishing. Hon members will appreciate the fact that of the population of some 325,000 people in Newfoundland, some 30,000 are engaged in the fishing industry, scattered over the province in some 1,300 fishing communities. It will therefore be realized what an important factor the salt codfish industry is to the province.
I have read the statement of the minister today, and frankly I must confess to him that although I thank him for it, I do not feel entirely satisfied with it. I realize fully, of course, the position the department was up against. But in so far as I am concerned, whilst the statement is appreciated it does not go far enough and it does not answer the worries that the people engaged in the fisheries in the province of Newfoundland wish answered. Actually all that has happened is this. The government is to buy at two-thirds of the 1948 price the amount of fish in the hands of the fishermen. As the

Supply-Fisheries
minister stated, that amount is comparatively small. The minister may feel like telling the amount but I am not going to press him to do so. Neither am I going to ask him what amount of fish is still in the hands of merchants and exporters in Newfoundland. I do not think that amount of fish should be disclosed. It may interfere with future marketing, and I certainly have no intention of putting that question to him.
With all due respect to the fisheries prices support board and their recommendation, I suggest that their recommendation is not a sound one. As the minister well knows, the fishing industry in Newfoundland is carried on under a system that is unique, having regard to the rest of the dominion. It is largely a credit business. Fishermen do not go fishing until they have been given supplies by the merchants in the various settlements before the fishing begins. As I am quite certain the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay will agree, having surplus fish in the hands' of merchants, particularly where the capital of the merchants is not great, is going to preclude the giving of supplies to fishermen. With all due respect to the advice the minister has received, I feel it is not quite the answer to the problem. I feel that there is a real emergency in the province at the present time, and I feel that there should be given a definite undertaking to buy at least the amount of fish that was left over, that could not be sold and that will not be sold in the ordinary manner and through the ordinary channels at the end of the year. If that is not given then I fear very much for the supplying that is going to take place this year. I realize of course that they are going to fish because Newfoundland people are usually independent, but if the needed money is not in the merchant's hands to grant supplies then I do not know how it is expected that the ordinary fisherman is going to be able to go fishing. I say that with all due respect to the particular committee that made the recommendations to the minister.
I have eight particular things that I want to discuss with the minister. The second one is the question I put to him this morning, namely, arranging the convertibility of sterling for the sale of salt codfish up to 400,000 quintals. To bear out what I said this morning I want to read two or three excerpts from newspaper accounts at the time the explanation was made. The first one is dated April 24, and is from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. It reads;	.
The government of Canada will aid Newfoundland in selling her salt codfish to Europe over the

sterling-dollar exchange barriers during 1950, fisheries minister R. W. Mayiiew announced here today through Newfoundland fisheries board chairman Raymond Gushue.
It is understood1 that the federal government will provide the necessary exchange to enable Newfoundland to sell 400,000 quintals of codfish to Italy, Spain and Portugal.
On the same day, April 24, in the Evening Telegram of Newfoundland in big black headlines we find the following:
Federal government will help Newfoundland sell salt cod to Europe
The government of Canada will aid Newfoundland in selling her codfish to Europe over the sterling-dollar exchange barriers during 1950, fisheries minister R. W. Mayhew announced here Sunday through Newfoundland fisheries board chairman Raymond Gushue.
The report is practically the same as that which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. The statement is made in the issue of the Evening Telegram of April 26, and again on May 2 in an editorial in the Daily News of St. John's, beginning:
That Ottawa's undertaking to facilitate the marketing of 400,000 quintals of salt fish in Europe has not been sufficient to facilitate spring supply has been illustrated by the demands of many fishermen for guaranteed minimum prices.
The last one is the particular reference that I made this morning to the announcement by the acting chairman of the Newfoundland salt codfish association, and this is what he said:
As indicated in the recent statement brought back from Ottawa by Mr. R. Gushue, the federal government is sympathetic and is anxious to help find a solution to the problems, and that statement has been interpreted by Mr. Gushue to mean that the federal government will undertake to provide conversion to dollars for the sale in sterling areas of not over 400,000 quintals of the 1950 production of Newfoundland salt codfish.
Definitely, whatever the minister's views are in the matter now, that was the way the statement was interpreted and I hope that he may be able to clear up whatever confusion there may be in the matter.
The next matter to which I wish to refer is the question of trawlers. The minister has already made a statement on that matter. He has sent his largest boat, the Cygnus, to the banks. I do not know whether the minister is fully aware of the situation, and I am certainly not going to read all the newspaper clippings that I have because they are too numerous. But we start off with the statement of the Evening Telegram of June 12 headed, "Piracy on the Grand Banks". It gives a description of what has happened. Then we have another account describing the number of people that are fishing on the banks and who they are. This is from the Telegram of June 10:
Well, the result of many inquiries made by the Telegram during the past couple of days indicates

that close to two hundred, if not actually more, ships from Spain, France and Portugal have been on the banks at one time or another this year.
They range in size from tiny 58-ton Spanish trawlers which fish in pairs to the mammoth 1,000 tonners of which each of the European countries sends out many to the new world waters.
At present there are seventeen ships from Portugal.
There are forty-eight from France and I do not know how many from Spain, but they are quite numerous. There has been some very strong comment over the fact that crews have been losing lines. They have been losing their trawl lines. One fellow reported losing seventy. Another crew reported losing forty, and in one particular item it was reported that there was actually great danger to the fishermen in the dories. I know the minister is very serious about this matter. I hope that because of the provisions of the international northwest Atlantic fisheries convention which has been adopted by this parliament this year the situation will be taken care of in the future. If the minister is going to reply I would like him to tell me what will be done by this fisheries convention and what is proposed by Canada should be done.
Also in connection with these trawlers fishing the banks there comes the very vital matter of the depletion of the resources of the Grand Banks. In that connection I would refer the minister-I am sure he remembers it-to a statement made by him on March 21 on the first day's session of the meeting of the fisheries council of Canada. This is what he said at that time:
Our industry both for itself and for future fishermen must recognize the importance of such conservation work. On the Atlantic the European fishing fleets will by next year be 140 per cent above their pre-war capacity and they will be fishing more intensely the waters around our shores.

speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
I will not be long; you can carry me after that. At page 5 of the annual report of the fisheries research board of Canada for 1949 appears this statement:
Fisheries that are being studied for the purpose of detecting changes in abundance due to overfishing include the cod, haddock and other ground-fish off our east coast. Fishermen of many countries including the United States and several European countries (France, Spain, and Portugal), fish the Grand Banks, and waters even nearer our shores. Some believe that overfishing is taking place and that there should be international action for the control of fishing. Canada's stake in these fisheries is so great that we must have reliable information of our own as a basis for action to protect our interests in negotiations looking to the study and control of these fisheries. Such studies have been under way for a number of years but they must be expanded as rapidly as possible. Our responsibility for Newfoundland's fisheries has increased our responsibility in this regard.
Supply-Fisheries
I have just a couple more excerpts to conclude this matter of depletion. The Daily News of May 26 reads as follows:
Vast as are the fishing resources of the Grand Banks, they are not inexhaustible and it is consequently disturbing to hear of the damage that some trawlers have been doing to the grounds. The owner of a banking vessel has told recently how his schooner had to sail through a large area of water which was covered with young fish that had escaped from trawlers' nets or had been thrown overboard as too small for commercial use. That can hardly be good for the preservation of the banks as a first-class fishing reserve.
From the Telegram of March 24 I quote the following:
As soon as the war was over European trawlers began crossing the ocean in hundreds to fish the waters of the Atlantic. At the same time American trawlers moved north as the old Georges bank and other Yankee fishing grounds became depleted. All of them moved in on the fishing grounds which Newfoundland and Canadian fishermen had come to regard as their own.
At the same time these foreign fishermen were not too particular as to how they treated the grounds nor the Canadian fishermen. They'd sweep through nursery grounds, killing all the small fish on them, and they'd sweep straight through the gear of the Canadian fishermen, wrecking it completely.
It is on the subject of conservation that I hope the minister will make some comments because last year at the time of his estimates I believe he said there was no evidence at all to justify any contention that the fishing grounds were being over-fished. I hope he can give some guarantee this year. It would be interesting to hear it.
I should like him also to comment on the question of Labrador fisheries, in so far as Newfoundland is concerned. I believe there has been a suggestion that to continue that fishery would be impractical and uneconomical. There are so many persons in the province engaged in that fishery that unless there is a very clear statement as to why it would be uneconomical I fear it will continue to be prosecuted. I certainly would like to have the minister's views in the matter.
The next matter has already been raised by my colleague. It has to do with unemployment insurance for fishermen. I realize the difficulties there may be in this respect. However the situation which has developed in the new province is commented upon in the Daily News of April 18, from the Grand Banks on the south coast. Here is what they say:
It is reported that some of the bank fishermen have decided not to go fishing this year but are seeking other employment in which they can qualify for unemployment insurance. In interviews with some of the men who are going fishing it was learned that bank fishermen feel strongly about not being included in unemployment insurance. They argue that they are the primary producers of codfish and are not included in the insurance scheme, whilst the women and men ashore

Supply-Fisheries
who cure and handle the fish in preparing it for market are eligible and have been receiving benefits this past winter.
I would urge the minister to think over the possibility of making fishermen eligible to come under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The final matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention arises out of the marketing of salt codfish. I do not mean the actual selling of it, but the straight marketing. In a brief presented by the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited this selling agency expressed an opinion to the royal commission on transportation, I believe, and a particular reference was made to what was happening in connection with the transportation of fish to market.
I shall not delay too long in drawing to the minister's attention the chief points to which these Newfoundland salt codfish are sent. The first of these groups is (a) by direct vessel to Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Cuba, Dominica, Grenada, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and some three or four more. Then there is group (b), which includes transshipments via Halifax and/or New York.
In connection with group (a) the situation is that these are by locally-owned vessels, and they are required to pay 50 cents per cask over and above the regular freight rate. In class (b) the shippers are obliged to pay a freight rate which is based upon the regular rate from Halifax, plus the cost of movement from ports in Newfoundland to Halifax.
The general plea is that they ask that arrangements should be made whereby Newfoundland salt fish moving to markets under (b) should receive a freight concession on an equal basis to that granted movements of salt fish from points on the mainland to export points.
An additional charge of 50 cents a cask which many shippers are at present obliged to pay for the privilege of having direct vessels load at their port should be, at least in part, absorbed by the Canadian National Railways in accordance with the policy of providing special depressed rates to cover similar situations in other provinces, and because there are no facilities for the movement of fish by rail.
A very serious situation would arise in Newfoundland in the event of the direct vessels at present serving markets under (a) being withdrawn, or the rates increased.
I draw this to the minister's attention, because I believe he should be aware of it. That sums up what I had intended to say. All hon. members appreciate the work of the minister and of his assistants, and their great interest in the fishing industry. I am
[Mr. Higgins.l
sure when I bring these points to his attention he will understand that it is only because of the keen interest he has shown in the fisheries.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer some of these questions before they pile up ahead of me. Perhaps I might first reply to the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The hon. member for Skeena was right in the premise he took that the halibut commission had the authority only to recommend and not to regulate. We are quite prepared to enter into a treaty, so long as that treaty has in it that provision. But if it means that they want the power to regulate, then we do not think that as a federal government we can agree to it without becoming involved in provincial as well as marine law.
For instance, we would not want anyone to regulate the time our boats would leave or return to port. If the term "regulation" were changed to "recommendation" we might agree to such changes in the treaty as proposed.
One point was made which I think was a mistake. The impression was left that the department was confining the catch of halibut to thirty days. That is not so. We regulate by the amount of fish caught. In area 2 the quota set for this year is 25,500,000 pounds. That amount was caught this year in thirty days. In area 3 the quota is 28,000,000 pounds, and they will catch that amount in about sixty days. I might point out that in 1931 there were 328 vessels on the banks, whereas now there are 744. That is the reason they get this quantity of fish in such a short time. We have no regulation that they must be caught in one month. This is controlled rather by the number of boats on the banks. They catch the quota which has been set by the halibut commission.
We are now investigating whether there should be more fish caught, and whether the banks will allow us to continue to fish at that rate or at a greater rate. If the halibut commission believe that the fish are there, they can make a recommendation to us, and it will no doubt be carried out.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: What about the split season?

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
There is no reason why we
should say that we would not be prepared to recommend a split season. But what good would it do? You would work for fifteen days and catch your allotment and then lay up your boat for a month or so. You would then go out and fish for another fifteen days and catch another allotment. Unless we are prepared to increase the allotment I do not

see any sense at all in having a split season. The fishermen would not catch any more fish and their boats would be laid up for one or two months. As has been suggested by the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, investigations should be made and they are being made.
The hon. member for Charlotte referred to a problem in connection with sardines. We will ask the fisheries prices support board to take a look at the situation. But I would remind the hon. member that sardines and herring are unpredictable fish. Some years you are able to catch a lot of them and in other years you get very few. Some seasons the catch is so large that it is almost impossible to take care of it. We have been able to take care of a similar situation on the west coast by the use of reduction plants and possibly the same method could be used in other areas. At any rate we will have the fisheries prices support board look into this situation.
The hon. member for St. John's East referred to the statement I made today and intimated that I had not gone far enough. We followed the recommendations of the prices support board which I think were fair and reasonable. We are taking the fish from the fishermen for more than one reason. The fish were not cured until this spring and we are not sure whether or not they should go on the market. This will give us a chance to find out and to eliminate any that should not go on the market. One of the principles we try to maintain is to see that the quality of our fish is high because that is what the people want. Any fish of inferior quality that get on the market are a detriment to the rest. The amount involved is only 12,000 or 15,000 quintals, but we do not want even that small amount to get mixed up with the good stock now held by the merchants and processors. That stock is disappearing fairly rapidly and I do not think there will be any difficulty in disposing of it.
The hon. member then referred to the alleged statement made by Mr. Gushue. Mr. Gushue was authorized to say that the government of Canada would do everything in its power to see that the exchange difficulties with certain European countries would interfere as little as possible with the disposal of the 1950 catch. Hon. members will appreciate that arrangements of this kind are not solely in the hands of the Canadian government. The matter is under active discussion with the government of the United Kingdom and as soon as a definite announcement can be made the industry in Newfoundland will be informed. The negotiations are going on and for that reason we are not in position to say anything more about them.
Supply-Fisheries

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: I did not mean to say that Mr. Gushue made the statement. It was attributed to him.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
That is what I said. The hon. member referred also to piracy on the Grand Banks. Those waters are international and our own fishermen are down there just the same as the fishermen from Spain, Portugal and seven or eight other countries. We have no jurisdiction over those waters nor has the northwest Atlantic convention. They are concerned only with conservation. The rules of the road will be discussed this fall but that is quite a different matter from conservation.
Labrador fisheries were also mentioned. I may be wrong, but my understanding is that the Labrador fish is not equal in quality to the fish caught off the shores of Newfoundland. It is considered to be a second-grade fish and we feel that as far as possible the fish marketed should be of the highest quality and be caught where they can be caught most cheaply.
The matter of unemployment insurance for fishermen is being considered by the Department of Labour and is something with which we are not concerned. Freight rates are a responsibility of the Department of Transport, but we will see what can be done about them.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext: I thank the minister for the information he has given. Can he say anything about the depletion of the Grand Banks?

maintopic: QUESTIONS AS TO FINAL PAYMENT ON FIVE-YEAR POOL
speechtext:
Our biologists tell us that there is no evidence of depletion on the Grand Banks, and I think that they are right.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
